lessons.title: Hello, Python! Your First Program
lessons.explain: The print() function displays text on the screen. Text wrapped in quotes is called a string. This is the traditional first step in every programming language — and every Python journey.
takeaways: print() sends output to the screen — your program talking back to you.
Text in quotes ("..." or '...') is called a string.
Python runs top to bottom, one line at a time.
lessons.code:
print("Hello, Skillzify!")
print("I am learning Python 🚀")

quiz.q: What does print("Hi") do?
quiz.why: print() sends text to the program's output — usually your screen or console.

quiz.q: In Python, text wrapped in quotes is called a…
quiz.why: Quoted text is a string (str) — one of Python's core data types.

quiz.q: What does this print? print("Py", "thon")
quiz.why: print() separates multiple arguments with a space.

quiz.q: In this code, which line prints first? print("one") then print("two")
quiz.why: Python runs code top to bottom, one line at a time.

quiz.q: What is wrong with print(Hello)?
options: Hello must be in quotes to be a string
quiz.why: Without quotes, Python reads Hello as a variable name, which does not exist.

challenge.hint: With strings, + joins (concatenates) them instead of adding.

lessons.title: Variables & Data Types
lessons.explain: Variables store values under a name. Python figures out the type automatically — int for whole numbers, float for decimals, str for text, and bool for True/False. Think of a variable as a labelled box you can put things in and swap out later.
takeaways: Create a variable with name = value — no type declaration needed.
Core types: int, float, str, bool. Check with type().
Variable names use letters, digits, _ — and can't start with a digit.
lessons.code:
name = "Vikas"
age = 20
height = 5.9
is_student = True

print(name, age, height, is_student)
print(type(age))  # <class 'int'>

quiz.q: What is the type of x = 3.14?
quiz.why: A number with a decimal point is a float (floating-point).

quiz.q: Which is a valid variable name?
quiz.why: Names can't start with a digit, can't contain '-', and can't be Python keywords like class.

quiz.q: What does this print? x = 5, then x = x + 2, then print(x)
quiz.why: x is reassigned: 5 + 2 = 7.

quiz.q: Which assignment fails?
quiz.why: Hyphens are not allowed in names — Python reads it as subtraction.

quiz.q: After a = 10 and b = a, what is b?
quiz.why: b copies a's current value, which is 10.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank so the program prints 25:
challenge.code:
age = ____
print(age + 5)  # should print 25
challenge.hint: age + 5 = 25, so age must be the integer 20.

lessons.title: Strings & f-strings
lessons.explain: f-strings let you embed variables directly inside text using curly braces — just prefix the string with f. They're the cleanest, fastest way to build messages in modern Python, and you'll use them everywhere.
takeaways: Prefix a string with f to embed {expressions} inside it.
String methods like .upper(), .lower(), .strip() return new strings.
len(s) gives the number of characters in a string.
lessons.code:
name = "Vikas"
score = 95

message = f"{name} scored {score} marks!"
print(message)
print(name.upper())
print(len(name))

quiz.q: What does f"{name}!" do?
quiz.why: The f prefix turns {name} into the variable's value inside the string.

quiz.q: What is len("Python")?
quiz.why: P-y-t-h-o-n = 6 characters.

quiz.q: What does this print? s = "hello", then print(s.upper())
quiz.why: .upper() returns a new all-caps string.

quiz.q: What does this print? x = 5, then print(f"{x + 1}")
quiz.why: f-strings can evaluate any expression inside the braces.

quiz.q: After s = "abc" and s.upper(), what is s?
quiz.why: String methods return new strings; they never change the original.

challenge.code:
s = "abc"
print(s.upper() + str(len(s)))
challenge.hint: s.upper() → "ABC", len(s) → 3, str(3) → "3", then + joins them.

lessons.title: Conditionals: if / elif / else
lessons.explain: Conditionals let your program make decisions. Python checks each condition top to bottom and runs the first block that is True. Indentation (4 spaces) defines which lines belong to each block — get it wrong and Python complains.
takeaways: if / elif / else chain: first True condition wins, the rest are skipped.
Conditions use comparisons: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=
Indentation is syntax in Python — it defines code blocks.

quiz.q: With marks = 82, what prints?
quiz.why: 82 >= 90 is False, 82 >= 75 is True → the elif branch runs.

quiz.q: Which keyword tests another condition after if?
quiz.why: elif is short for 'else if' — Python's own keyword.

quiz.q: What prints? x = 5, if x > 10: print("big"), else: print("small")
quiz.why: 5 > 10 is False, so the else branch runs.

quiz.q: In an if / elif / else chain, how many branches run?
quiz.why: Python runs the first branch whose condition is true, then skips the rest.

quiz.q: What is wrong with: if score = 100: ?
quiz.why: = stores a value; == compares two values.

challenge.hint: These are two separate if statements — both conditions are True, so both run.

lessons.title: Loops: for & while
lessons.explain: Loops repeat work without repeating code. A for loop walks through a sequence — range(n) gives 0 … n-1. A while loop repeats while its condition stays True. The classic beginner bug: a while loop whose condition never becomes False runs forever!
takeaways: for i in range(5) loops with i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
while repeats while its condition is True — make sure it can end.
break exits a loop immediately; continue skips to the next round.
lessons.code:
print("For loop:")
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(f"  2 x {i} = {2 * i}")

print("While loop:")
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(f"  Countdown: {count}")
    count -= 1
print("Go! 🚀")

quiz.q: What numbers does range(1, 6) produce?
quiz.why: range(start, stop) includes start but stops before stop.

quiz.q: What does break do inside a loop?
quiz.why: break jumps straight out of the loop. (continue skips to the next iteration.)

quiz.q: What does this print? for i in range(3): print(i)
quiz.why: range(3) starts at 0 and stops before 3.

quiz.q: What makes while True: dangerous?
options: It loops forever unless break runs
quiz.why: True never becomes False, so only break can stop it.

quiz.q: What prints? for i in range(5): if i == 2: continue, then print(i)
quiz.why: continue skips the rest of that round, so 2 is never printed.

challenge.code:
total = 0
for i in range(4):
    total += i
print(total)

lessons.title: Lists & Tuples
lessons.explain: Lists let you keep an ordered collection of items you can change — perfect for things like to-do lists or scores. Tuples look similar but are locked after creation, which makes them great for fixed data like coordinates. Knowing when to use each one is a core Python habit.
takeaways: Lists are ordered and changeable — index them from 0, or from -1 for the end.
append() adds to the end; slicing like [1:3] grabs a sub-list.
Tuples are immutable — use them for fixed data you do not want accidentally changed.
lessons.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("mango")
print(fruits[0])
print(fruits[1:3])
point = (3, 4)
print(point)

quiz.q: What does fruits.append("mango") do?
options: Adds mango to the end of the list
Replaces the first item with mango
quiz.why: append() always adds the new item at the end of the list.

quiz.q: What happens if you try point[0] = 5 on a tuple?
quiz.why: Tuples are immutable, so item assignment raises a TypeError.

quiz.q: What does this print? fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"], then print(fruits[1:3])
quiz.why: Slicing [1:3] takes indices 1 and 2.

quiz.q: What does this print? a = [1, 2], b = a, b.append(3), print(a)
quiz.why: b refers to the same list object as a, so the change is visible through a.
The tuple holds two items.

challenge.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
print(nums[-1])
challenge.hint: Negative indexes count from the end of the list.

lessons.title: Dictionaries & Sets
lessons.explain: Dictionaries store data as key-value pairs, so you can look things up by name instead of by position — like a real dictionary. Sets are unordered collections that automatically drop duplicates, which makes them perfect for membership tests. Together they power everything from counting words to removing repeats.
takeaways: Dictionaries map keys to values; look up with d[key] or the safer d.get(key, default).
Assigning to a new key adds it; assigning to an existing key updates it.
Sets store unique items only — duplicates vanish automatically.

quiz.q: What does student.get("grade", "N/A") return when "grade" is missing?
quiz.why: .get() returns the default you supply instead of raising a KeyError.

quiz.q: Why does {"red", "blue", "red"} end up with only two items?
options: The last item overwrites the first
quiz.why: A set can only hold unique values, so the repeated "red" is dropped.

quiz.q: What does this print? d = {"x": 1}, d["x"] = 9, print(d["x"])
quiz.why: Assigning to an existing key overwrites its value.

quiz.q: "z" in {"a", "b"} is…
quiz.why: in tests membership, and "z" is not in the set.

quiz.q: What does this print? s = {3, 1, 2}, print(len(s))
quiz.why: The set holds three unique items.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank so the program prints 21:
challenge.hint: Dictionary keys go inside the square brackets.

lessons.title: Conditionals & Logic
lessons.explain: Programs get smart when they can make decisions, and conditionals are how you teach them. if/elif/else lets your code take different paths based on what is true right now. Combined with and, or, and not, you can express surprisingly subtle logic in just a few lines.
takeaways: if/elif/else runs the first branch whose condition is true.
and needs both sides true; or needs just one; not flips a condition.
Comparisons can chain: 1 < x < 10 checks both ends at once.

quiz.q: What prints when score is 85?
quiz.why: 85 is not >= 90, but it is >= 75, so the elif branch runs.

quiz.q: In "if x > 5 and x < 10:", when does the block run?
options: Only when both conditions are true
quiz.why: and requires the left and right conditions to both be true.

quiz.q: What does this print? x = 7, print(1 < x < 10)
quiz.why: Chained comparisons check both ends: 1 < 7 and 7 < 10.

quiz.q: not (5 > 3) is…
quiz.why: 5 > 3 is True, and not flips it to False.

quiz.q: What prints? age = 16, print("teen" if 13 <= age <= 19 else "other")
quiz.why: 16 is between 13 and 19, so the condition is True.

challenge.hint: 30 is greater than 25, so the first branch runs.

lessons.title: Loops: for & while
lessons.explain: Loops let you repeat work without repeating code — the moment a program needs to do something a hundred times, you need them. for loops walk through collections and ranges, while while loops keep going until a condition changes. break and continue give you fine control over when to stop or skip.
takeaways: for i in range(n) loops n times with i going 0 to n-1.
while repeats until its condition becomes false — make sure it eventually does.
break exits the loop now; continue skips to the next round.
lessons.code:
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)
    count = count - 1
print("Go!")

quiz.q: What does range(3) produce?
quiz.why: range(3) starts at 0 and stops before 3.

quiz.q: What does break do inside a loop?
quiz.why: break exits the loop right away; continue is the one that skips ahead.

quiz.q: What does this print? total = 0, for i in range(1, 4): total += i, print(total)
n starts at 3 and a while n > 0 loop does n -= 1 each round. How many rounds run?
quiz.why: n goes 3, 2, 1, then 0 stops the loop — 3 rounds.

quiz.q: What prints? for c in "ab": print(c)
quiz.why: for walks through each character of the string in order.

challenge.code:
total = 0
for n in [1, 2, 3]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
challenge.hint: Add them up step by step: 0+1, then +2, then +3.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.explain: Functions let you package logic into reusable, named blocks — write once, call anywhere. Parameters make them flexible, return values make them useful, and default arguments make them friendly. Good functions are the difference between a script and a program.
takeaways: def names a function; parameters are its inputs, return sends a result back.
Arguments with defaults (name="friend") are optional when calling.
A function without return gives back None.
lessons.code:
def greet(name="friend"):
    return "Hello, " + name

print(greet("Asha"))
print(greet())

quiz.q: What does return do in a function?
options: Sends a value back to the caller
quiz.why: return hands a value back to whoever called the function.

quiz.q: What prints for greet() with no arguments?
quiz.why: The default "friend" is used when no argument is given.

quiz.q: What does this print? def double(n): return n * 2, then print(double(5))
quiz.why: double(5) returns 10, which print displays.

quiz.q: With def add(a, b=0):, which call is valid?
quiz.why: b has a default, so only a is required.

quiz.q: What is wrong with a def line that has no colon at the end?
options: Missing colon after the def line
quiz.why: def lines must end with a colon before the indented body.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank so the program prints 12:
challenge.hint: The function must send the result back to the caller.

lessons.title: Numbers & Math in Python
lessons.explain: Python does arithmetic the way you expect, plus a few bonus operators: // for floor division, % for the remainder, and ** for powers. Whole numbers are ints, decimals are floats, and mixing them always gives a float.
takeaways: `//` divides and rounds down, `%` gives the remainder — together they split totals, like minutes into hours and minutes.
`**` raises to a power: `2 ** 10` is 1024.
Mixing an int and a float always gives a float: `3 + 0.5` is `3.5`.
lessons.code:
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(7 % 2)
print(2 ** 4)

quiz.q: What does `print(10 % 3)` output?
quiz.why: 10 divided by 3 is 3 with remainder 1, and % gives the remainder.

quiz.q: What is the value of `2 ** 3`?
quiz.why: ** means 'to the power of': 2 * 2 * 2 = 8.

quiz.q: What type is the result of `4 + 1.5`?
quiz.why: Adding an int and a float always produces a float.

challenge.code: print(2 ** 3)
challenge.hint: ** means 'to the power of', not multiplication.

lessons.title: String Methods You Will Use Daily
lessons.explain: Strings come with built-in tools called methods. Just a few — strip(), upper(), replace(), split() and join() — handle most everyday text jobs like cleaning up input or building messages.
takeaways: String methods return a NEW string; the original never changes, so write `s = s.strip()`.
`split()` breaks text into a list; `' '.join(parts)` glues a list back into text.
`strip()` removes whitespace from both ends — perfect for tidying user input.
lessons.code:
name = "  Ada  "
print(name.strip())
print(name.strip().upper())
words = "red,blue,green".split(",")
print(words)

quiz.q: What does `'  hello  '.strip()` return?
quiz.why: strip() removes the whitespace from both ends, leaving 'hello'.

quiz.q: After `s = 'a,b,c'` and `parts = s.split(',')`, what is `parts`?
quiz.why: split(',') cuts the string at each comma into a list of three items.

quiz.q: Does `'Hi'.upper()` change the original string?
options: No — strings are immutable, it returns a new one
Yes, it edits the string in place
Only if you assign it back
quiz.why: Strings can't be changed in place; upper() builds and returns a new string.

challenge.code: print("one two".split())
challenge.hint: split() with no arguments splits on any whitespace.

lessons.title: Slicing & Indexing Strings
lessons.explain: Every character in a string has a position starting at 0. Indexing with s[i] grabs one character, and slicing with s[start:stop] grabs a range — the start is included but the stop is left out.
takeaways: Indexes start at 0; negative indexes count from the end, so `s[-1]` is the last character.
In `s[start:stop]`, start is included but stop is excluded.
`s[::-1]` reverses a string — a trick worth memorizing.
lessons.code:
s = "Python"
print(s[0])
print(s[-1])
print(s[0:4])
print(s[::-1])

quiz.q: If `s = 'Python'`, what is `s[1]`?
quiz.why: Counting starts at 0, so index 1 is the second character, 'y'.

quiz.q: What does `'Python'[1:4]` give?
quiz.why: It takes indexes 1, 2 and 3 ('y', 't', 'h'); index 4 is excluded.

quiz.q: What is the value of `'abc'[-1]`?
quiz.why: Negative indexes count from the end, so -1 is the last character.

challenge.code: print('hello'[1:4])
challenge.hint: Counting starts at 0, and the stop index is left out.

lessons.title: List Methods in Depth
lessons.explain: Lists are mutable, and their methods change them in place. append() adds one item to the end, extend() adds many, insert() squeezes one in at a position, remove() deletes by value, and pop() takes an item out and hands it back.
takeaways: `append()` adds ONE item; `extend()` adds EACH item of another list.
`pop()` removes AND returns an item; `remove()` deletes by value.
Most list methods return None — the change happens to the list itself.
lessons.code:
nums = [1, 2]
nums.append(3)
nums.extend([4, 5])
print(nums)
print(nums.pop())
print(nums)

quiz.q: After `a = [1, 2]` and `a.append([3, 4])`, what is `a`?
quiz.why: append() adds its argument as a single item, so the list becomes nested.

quiz.q: What does `[10, 20, 30].pop(0)` return?
quiz.why: pop(0) removes and returns the item at index 0, which is 10.

quiz.q: Which removes the FIRST occurrence of the value 5 from `lst`?
quiz.why: remove() deletes by value; pop() works by index instead.

challenge.code:
a = [10, 20]
a.append(30)
print(len(a))
challenge.hint: len() counts items, and append() added one more.

lessons.title: Tuples: Unpacking & Immutability
lessons.explain: A tuple is like a list you can't change — perfect for fixed data like coordinates or RGB colors. You can unpack a tuple into separate variables in one line, which makes swaps and multiple values elegant.
takeaways: Tuples are immutable: you can't add, remove, or change items after creation.
Unpacking assigns each item to its own variable: `x, y = (3, 4)`.
Use tuples for data that should never change, like coordinates or dates.
lessons.code:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x + y)
print((x, y))

quiz.q: What happens when you run `(1, 2).append(3)`?
options: It works just like a list
quiz.why: Tuples are immutable and have no append method at all.

quiz.q: After `a, b = (5, 9)`, what is `a + b`?
quiz.why: Unpacking gives a = 5 and b = 9, so a + b is 14.

quiz.q: Why choose a tuple over a list?
options: To protect data from accidental changes
Tuples are always faster to type
quiz.why: Immutability is a feature: it guarantees the data stays exactly as created.

challenge.code:
x, y = (10, 20)
print(y - x)
challenge.hint: After unpacking, y is 20 and x is 10.

lessons.title: Dictionary Methods in Depth
lessons.explain: Dictionaries store key-value pairs, and their methods make lookups safe and iteration easy. get() avoids KeyError crashes, keys()/values()/items() expose the contents, and update() merges another dictionary in.
takeaways: `d.get(key, default)` returns the default instead of crashing when a key is missing.
`d.items()` lets you loop over key AND value together: `for k, v in d.items()`.
`setdefault()` inserts a key only if it isn't already there.

quiz.q: What does `{}.get('x', 'none')` return?
quiz.why: The key is missing, so get() returns the default you supplied.

quiz.q: Which loop prints both keys and values of `d`?
quiz.why: items() yields (key, value) pairs, which unpack neatly into k and v.

quiz.q: After `d = {'a': 1}` and `d.update({'b': 2})`, what is `d`?
quiz.why: update() merges the new pairs into the existing dictionary.

challenge.code:
d = {"x": 1}
print(d.get("y"))
challenge.hint: get() without a default returns None for missing keys.

lessons.title: Set Operations: Union, Intersection & Difference
lessons.explain: Sets hold unique items and support math-style operations. Union (|) combines everything from both sets, intersection (&) keeps only what's in both, and difference (-) keeps what's only in the first.
takeaways: Sets automatically drop duplicates: `set([1, 1, 2])` is `{1, 2}`.
`a | b` is the union, `a & b` the intersection, `a - b` the difference.
Use a set for fast membership tests or to remove duplicates from a list.

quiz.why: Union combines all unique items from both sets.

quiz.q: What does `{1, 2, 3} & {2, 4}` give?
quiz.why: Intersection keeps only items present in BOTH sets — just 2.

quiz.q: What is `len(set([5, 5, 5, 6]))`?
quiz.why: Duplicates collapse, leaving {5, 6}, which has 2 items.

challenge.hint: Difference keeps the items NOT in the second set.

lessons.title: Type Conversion & the input() Function
lessons.explain: input() always returns text, even when the user types a number — so convert it with int() or float() before doing math. The same conversion functions switch between types anywhere: int('7') becomes 7, str(7) becomes '7'.
takeaways: `input()` returns a string — wrap it: `age = int(input('Age: '))`.
`int('7')` gives 7, `str(7)` gives '7', `float('2.5')` gives 2.5.
Converting bad text like `int('abc')` raises a ValueError.
lessons.code:
age_text = "21"
age = int(age_text)
print(age + 4)
print("Next year: " + str(age + 1))

quiz.q: If `n = input()` and the user types 5, what does `n + 1` do?
options: Raises TypeError — can't add int to str
quiz.why: n is the string '5', and adding a string and an int is a TypeError.

quiz.q: What does `int('42') + 8` equal?
quiz.why: int('42') becomes the number 42 first, then 42 + 8 = 50.

quiz.q: What does `str(3.5)` return?
quiz.why: str() converts the float into its text form, '3.5'.

challenge.code: print(int("10") * 2)
challenge.hint: int('10') becomes the number 10 before the multiplication.

lessons.title: Boolean Logic: and, or, not
lessons.explain: and, or and not combine True/False values into decisions. `and` needs both sides true, `or` needs just one, and `not` flips a value — they're the building blocks of every if statement with multiple conditions.
takeaways: `and` is True only when BOTH sides are True; `or` needs just ONE.
`not` flips a value: `not True` is False.
Comparisons return booleans, so `age >= 18 and has_ticket` reads like English.
lessons.code:
age = 20
has_ticket = True
print(age >= 18 and has_ticket)
print(age < 13 or not has_ticket)

quiz.q: What is `True and False`?
quiz.why: and needs both sides True, but one side is False.

quiz.q: What is `True or False`?
quiz.why: or needs only one side True, and the left side is True.

quiz.q: What does `not (5 > 3)` evaluate to?
quiz.why: 5 > 3 is True, and not flips it to False.

challenge.code:
x = 7
print(x > 5 and x < 10)
challenge.hint: Is 7 both greater than 5 AND less than 10?

lessons.title: Nested Loops & Patterns
lessons.explain: A loop inside another loop runs the inner loop fully for every single step of the outer one. That's exactly what you need to draw grids and patterns — think of the outer loop as rows and the inner loop as columns.
takeaways: The inner loop completes ALL its iterations for each ONE iteration of the outer loop.
Use `print(..., end='')` to stay on the same line; a bare `print()` moves down a row.
Outer loop = rows, inner loop = columns is the mental model for patterns.

quiz.q: How many times does print run here? `for i in range(2):` then `for j in range(3): print(j)`
quiz.why: The inner loop runs 3 times for each of the 2 outer iterations: 2 x 3 = 6.

quiz.q: What does `print('a', end='')` followed by `print('b')` output?
options: a then b on separate lines
quiz.why: end='' replaces the newline, so 'b' prints right after 'a'.

quiz.q: In a pattern program, the outer loop usually represents…
quiz.why: Each outer iteration draws one full row; the inner loop draws its columns.

challenge.code:
for i in range(2):
    print(i, end="-")
challenge.hint: end='-' replaces the newline after each print.

lessons.title: break, continue & Loop else
lessons.explain: break exits a loop immediately, continue skips to the next iteration, and a loop's else block runs only if the loop finished without break — perfect for 'search and not found' logic.
takeaways: `break` stops the whole loop; `continue` skips just the current round.
A `for...else` runs its else only when NO break happened.
Use break for 'found it, stop looking' searches.

quiz.q: What does `break` do inside a loop?
quiz.why: break jumps straight out of the loop; nothing after it in the loop runs.

quiz.q: When does a `for...else` block's else run?
options: Only if the loop never hit break
Only if the loop body is empty
quiz.why: The else means 'completed normally' — a break skips it.

quiz.q: What prints? `for i in range(5):` `if i == 2: continue` `print(i, end='')`
quiz.why: continue skips only the iteration where i is 2; the rest print.

challenge.hint: The loop stops the moment i becomes 2.

lessons.title: Function Arguments: Defaults & Keywords
lessons.explain: Parameters can have default values, so callers may skip them — and any argument can be passed by name (keyword), which makes calls readable and frees you from remembering the order.
takeaways: A default like `def greet(name='friend')` makes that argument optional.
Keyword arguments name the parameter: `greet(name='Ada')`.
Once a parameter has a default, every parameter after it needs one too.
lessons.code:
def greet(name, punct="!"):
    print("Hi " + name + punct)
greet("Ada")
greet("Bob", punct="?")
greet(name="Zoe", punct=".")

quiz.q: Given `def f(a, b=5)`, which call is valid?
quiz.why: f(1) sets a=1 and b falls back to 5; the others break argument rules.

quiz.q: What is `greet(name='Ada')` using?
quiz.why: Naming the parameter at the call site is a keyword argument.

quiz.q: Why is `def f(a=1, b):` invalid?
options: A non-default parameter can't follow a default one
quiz.why: Python requires all defaulted parameters to come after the required ones.

challenge.hint: b falls back to its default of 10.

lessons.title: Scope: Local vs Global
lessons.explain: A variable created inside a function is local — it exists only while the function runs. Code outside can't see it, and a local with the same name as a global shadows (hides) it without changing the original.
takeaways: Local variables die when the function returns; they can't be used outside.
Reading a global inside a function is fine; assigning to it creates a NEW local unless you write `global`.
Same name inside and outside? The inner one wins — but only inside.
lessons.code:
x = 10
def show():
    x = 99
    print(x)
show()
print(x)

quiz.q: What prints? `x = 1` then `def f():` `x = 2` then `f()` then `print(x)`
quiz.why: The x inside f() is a separate local; the global x stays 1.

quiz.q: Can code outside a function read a variable created inside it?
options: No — it is local to the function
Only if it holds a number
quiz.why: Local variables exist only during the function's execution.

quiz.q: What does the `global` keyword do?
options: Lets a function assign to a module-level variable
quiz.why: Without it, assignment inside a function creates a local instead.

challenge.code:
n = 5
def change():
    n = 0
change()
print(n)
challenge.hint: The n inside change() is a separate local variable.

lessons.title: Docstrings & Getting Help
lessons.explain: A docstring is a triple-quoted string right under a function's def line that documents what it does. Python's help() shows it, and good docstrings make your future self (and teammates) grateful.
takeaways: A docstring is the FIRST statement in a function, written in triple quotes.
`help(func)` prints the docstring; `func.__doc__` gives it as a string.
One line for what it does, plus the parameters, is enough for small functions.
lessons.code:
def square(n):
    """Return n multiplied by itself."""
    return n * n
print(square.__doc__)

quiz.q: Where does a docstring go?
options: As the first statement inside the function
At the end of the file
quiz.why: Python treats the first string literal in a function body as its documentation.

quiz.q: What does `help(len)` do?
quiz.why: help() displays the docstring and signature of any object.

quiz.q: Which follows the docstring convention?
quiz.why: A triple-quoted string as the first statement is the documented convention.

challenge.prompt: Fill in the blank to print the function's docstring:
challenge.code:
def add(a, b):
    """Add a and b."""
    return a + b
print(____)
challenge.hint: Docstrings live in the __doc__ attribute.

lessons.title: The random Module: Build a Guessing Game
lessons.explain: The random module adds unpredictability: randint(a, b) picks an integer in a range, choice(seq) picks one item, and shuffle() mixes a list in place. Together they're all you need for games and simulations.
takeaways: `random.randint(1, 10)` can return 1 AND 10 — both ends are included.
`random.choice(['a', 'b'])` picks one item from a sequence.
`random.shuffle(deck)` shuffles in place and returns None.
lessons.code:
import random
print(random.randint(1, 6))
print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))
deck = [1, 2, 3]
random.shuffle(deck)
print(deck)

quiz.q: What values can `random.randint(1, 3)` return?
quiz.why: randint includes BOTH endpoints, unlike range().

quiz.q: What does `random.shuffle(cards)` return?
options: None — it shuffles the list in place
quiz.why: shuffle() mutates the list directly and returns None.

quiz.q: Which picks one random item from a list?
quiz.why: choice() is the real function; the others don't exist.

challenge.prompt: What will this print? (seed() makes randomness repeatable)
challenge.code:
import random
random.seed(42)
x = random.randint(1, 10)
random.seed(42)
y = random.randint(1, 10)
print(x == y)
challenge.hint: Same seed, same 'random' numbers.

lessons.title: Dates & Times with datetime
lessons.explain: The datetime module handles dates and times: date.today() gives you today, timedelta does date arithmetic like '7 days from now', and strftime() formats a date into any string layout you like.
takeaways: `from datetime import date, timedelta`, then `date.today()` is today's date.
Add `timedelta(days=7)` to a date to jump a week forward.
`strftime('%d %b %Y')` formats a date like '03 Nov 2026'.
lessons.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
today = date.today()
print(today)
print(today + timedelta(days=7))

quiz.q: What does `date.today() + timedelta(days=1)` give?
quiz.why: Adding a one-day timedelta moves the date one day forward.

quiz.q: What type of object does `date.today()` return?
quiz.why: It returns a date object, which you can format or do math with.

quiz.q: How many days are in `timedelta(weeks=2)`?
quiz.why: weeks=2 is converted to 14 days internally.

challenge.code:
from datetime import date
print(date(2026, 1, 1).strftime("%A"))
challenge.hint: %A is the full weekday name — New Year's Day 2026 is a Thursday.

lessons.title: None & Checking for Nothing
lessons.explain: None is Python's way of saying 'no value here' — it's also what every function returns when it doesn't return anything. Always check for it with `is None`, never with `==`, because `is` tests identity.
takeaways: `None` means 'no value'; a function without return gives back None.
Check with `is None` / `is not None` — not `==`.
`None` is falsy, so `if result:` catches it too — but `is None` is explicit.
lessons.code:
def find_user(name):
    return None
user = find_user("ada")
print(user is None)
print(user)

quiz.q: What does this return? `def f():` followed by `x = 1` (no return statement)
quiz.why: A function without return always gives back None.

quiz.q: Which is the correct None check?
quiz.why: is tests identity, which is the reliable way to check for None.

quiz.q: What is `bool(None)`?
quiz.why: None is falsy, like 0 and empty collections.

challenge.code:
x = None
print(x is None)
challenge.hint: is checks identity — x really is None.

lessons.title: Comments & Clean Code Style
lessons.explain: Comments (#) explain WHY your code does something, not what — the code already says what. Clean style (clear names, blank lines between ideas, short lines) makes code readable for humans, including future you.
takeaways: Write comments for the WHY, not the WHAT: `# retry: the API is flaky`.
Use descriptive names (`total_price`) over cryptic ones (`tp`).
Python ignores everything after `#` on a line — handy for quick experiments.
lessons.code:
# convert minutes into hours and leftover minutes
mins = 135
hours = mins // 60
left = mins % 60
print(hours, left)

quiz.q: Which comment is most useful?
options: # retry 3 times: the API is flaky on weekends
quiz.why: It explains WHY the code exists — the code itself already shows the what.

quiz.q: What does Python do with text after `#`?
quiz.why: Everything from # to the end of the line is a comment.

quiz.q: Which variable name is cleanest?
quiz.why: Descriptive names read like English and need no decoding.

challenge.code:
print("a")
# print("b")
print("c")
challenge.hint: Lines starting with # never run.

lessons.title: Reading Tracebacks: Debugging Basics
lessons.explain: When Python crashes it prints a traceback — read it BOTTOM-UP. The last line names the error (like NameError or TypeError), and the lines above show exactly where it happened. Most bugs are found in seconds once you read tracebacks this way.
takeaways: Read tracebacks bottom-up: the LAST line is the actual error.
`NameError` = misspelled or undefined name; `TypeError` = wrong kind of operation.
The `line N` part pinpoints exactly where it broke.

quiz.q: Where is the most useful line of a traceback?
options: The last line — it names the error
quiz.why: The final line states the error type and message; work upward from there.

quiz.q: What error does `print(5 + 'a')` raise?
quiz.why: Adding an int and a str is an operation on the wrong types.

quiz.q: What error does `print(x)` raise if x was never defined?
quiz.why: Using a name that doesn't exist is a NameError.

challenge.hint: Index 5 doesn't exist in a 2-item list, so IndexError is raised and caught.

lessons.title: Capstone: Command-Line To-Do App
lessons.explain: Time to put it all together: a to-do app using a list of dictionaries, one function per action, and a loop for the menu. This is how small real programs are structured — data plus functions plus a main loop.
takeaways: Model each to-do as a dict (`{'task': ..., 'done': False}`) inside a list.
One function per action (add, list, complete) keeps the program organized.
A `while True` loop with `break` on 'quit' is the classic menu pattern.
lessons.code:
todos = []

def add(task):
    todos.append({"task": task, "done": False})

add("Study Python")
add("Build app")
todos[0]["done"] = True
print(len(todos), "tasks,", sum(1 for t in todos if t["done"]), "done")

quiz.q: How is each to-do stored in the capstone app?
options: As a dict inside a list
quiz.why: Each to-do is a dict with 'task' and 'done' keys, collected in a list.

quiz.q: How does the menu loop exit?
options: break when the user chooses quit
quiz.why: The classic pattern is `while True` with `break` on the quit choice.

quiz.q: Why write one function per action?
options: Each piece is testable and readable on its own
quiz.why: Small functions are easier to understand, test, and reuse.

challenge.prompt: How many tasks are done here?
challenge.code:
tasks = [{"t": "a", "done": True}, {"t": "b", "done": False}]
print(sum(1 for t in tasks if t["done"]))
challenge.hint: Only one dict has done set to True.

lessons.title: Functions & Return Values
lessons.explain: Functions package reusable logic under a name. def defines one, parameters receive input, and return sends a result back to the caller. Default parameters (like greeting="Hello") make arguments optional — callers can skip them.
takeaways: def name(params): defines a function; call it with name(args).
return sends a value back. Without it, a function returns None.
Default parameters make arguments optional.
lessons.code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print(greet("Vikas"))
print(greet("Sara", greeting="Welcome"))
print("Sum:", add(7, 5))

quiz.q: What does return do?
options: Sends a value back to the caller
quiz.why: return hands a value back to whoever called the function; print just displays it.

quiz.q: In def greet(name, greeting="Hello"), greeting is…
quiz.why: It has a default value, so callers may omit it.

quiz.q: What does this print? def add(a, b): return a + b, then print(add(2, 3))
quiz.why: add(2, 3) returns 5, which print displays.

quiz.q: What does a function without return give back?
quiz.why: Falling off the end of a function returns None.

quiz.q: What does this print? def greet(name, greeting="Hello"): return greeting + " " + name, then print(greet("Sam"))
quiz.why: greeting falls back to its default, "Hello".

challenge.hint: b isn't given, so the default 10 is used: 5 + 10.

lessons.title: Lists, Tuples & Dictionaries
lessons.explain: Lists are ordered and changeable — your everyday workhorse. Tuples are ordered but frozen (great for fixed data like coordinates). Dictionaries map keys to values for fast lookups. These three cover most data you'll ever handle.
takeaways: Lists: ordered, mutable. Use append(), indexing, negative indices.
Tuples: ordered, immutable — safe for fixed collections.
Dicts: key → value pairs. Access with d[key], list keys with d.keys().
lessons.code:
skills = ["Python", "HTML", "CSS"]
skills.append("JavaScript")
print(skills[0], "→", skills[-1])

point = (18.5, 73.7)  # tuple: (lat, lon)
print("Pune coords:", point)

student = {"name": "Vikas", "track": "CSE", "cgpa": 8.6}
print(student["name"], "studies", student["track"])
print("Keys:", list(student.keys()))

quiz.q: Which of these is immutable?
quiz.why: Tuples can't be changed after creation — that's their whole point.

quiz.q: skills[-1] gives you…
quiz.why: Negative indices count from the end: -1 is the last item.

quiz.q: What does this print? d = {"a": 1}, d["b"] = 2, print(len(d))
quiz.why: Assigning a new key adds it, so the dict now has 2 entries.

quiz.q: What happens with t = (1, 2) followed by t.append(3)?
quiz.why: Tuples are immutable and have no append method.
Indexing starts at 0, so index 1 is the second item.

challenge.code:
d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
print(d["b"] + len(d))
challenge.hint: d["b"] is 2, and the dict has 2 keys → 2 + 2.

lessons.title: Error Handling with try/except
lessons.explain: Errors (exceptions) crash programs unless handled. Wrap risky code in try, catch specific problems with except, and use finally for cleanup that must always run. Handling specific errors beats a bare except — it keeps real bugs visible.
takeaways: try/except catches exceptions so your program survives them.
Catch specific errors (ZeroDivisionError) before general ones.
finally always runs — perfect for cleanup.

quiz.q: Without try/except, what happens on 10 / 0?
quiz.why: An unhandled exception terminates the program with a traceback.

quiz.q: A finally block…
quiz.why: finally executes whether or not an exception occurred.

quiz.q: What does this print? try: x = int("abc"), except ValueError: x = -1, then print(x)
quiz.why: int("abc") raises ValueError, which the except block catches.

quiz.q: Accessing a missing dict key raises…
quiz.why: Missing keys raise KeyError — catch that specifically.

quiz.q: What prints? try: print("a"), except: print("b"), else: print("c")
quiz.why: No error occurs, so try runs, then the else block runs.

challenge.hint: int("abc") raises ValueError, which the except catches.

lessons.title: OOP Basics: Classes & Objects
lessons.explain: Classes are blueprints; objects are the things built from them. __init__ runs when an object is created to set it up, self refers to the object itself, and methods are functions that belong to the class. OOP shines when you model real things with state + behaviour.
takeaways: class defines a blueprint; ClassName() creates an object (instance).
__init__ initialises each object; self is the object itself.
Methods are functions inside the class that operate on the object.
lessons.code:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name, track):
        self.name = name
        self.track = track
        self.xp = 0

    def complete_lesson(self, points=10):
        self.xp += points
        return f"{self.name} earned {points} XP (total {self.xp})"

s = Student("Vikas", "CSE")
print(s.complete_lesson())
print(s.complete_lesson(20))

quiz.q: What is self inside a method?
options: A reference to the object itself
quiz.why: self is how a method talks about the specific object it's working on.

quiz.q: Which method sets up a new object?
quiz.why: __init__ (the constructor) runs automatically when you create an object.

quiz.q: What does this print? class Cat: def __init__(self, n): self.n = n, then c = Cat("Tom"), print(c.n)
quiz.why: __init__ stores "Tom" in self.n.

quiz.q: What does Dog("Rex") do?
quiz.why: Calling the class name constructs a new object.

quiz.q: Why does Dog.bark() fail while rex.bark() works?
options: The instance isn't passed, so self has no value
quiz.why: Calling a method on an instance supplies self automatically.

challenge.hint: __init__ stored "Rex" in d.name.

lessons.title: Recursion: Functions That Call Themselves
lessons.explain: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of it. Every recursion needs two parts: a base case where it stops, and a recursive step that shrinks the problem. Miss the base case and you get infinite recursion → RecursionError.
takeaways: Base case: the stopping condition. Recursive step: call with smaller input.
Recursion is natural for trees, nested data, divide-and-conquer.
Python limits recursion depth (~1000) — loops suit very deep repetition.

quiz.q: What stops a recursive function from running forever?
quiz.why: The base case is the condition where the function returns instead of calling itself.

quiz.q: factorial(3) equals…
What does this print? def f(n): if n <= 0: return 0, return n + f(n-1), then print(f(3))
In a countdown function, the recursive step is…
quiz.why: It is the self-call with a smaller argument.

quiz.q: Why does def bad(n): return bad(n) crash?
options: No base case — it recurses forever
quiz.why: Every call makes another identical call until Python hits the recursion limit.

lessons.title: File Handling: Read & Write Files
lessons.explain: Files let programs remember things permanently. open(path, mode) opens a file: "w" writes (overwrites!), "r" reads, "a" appends. Always use the with statement — Python then closes the file automatically, even if an error strikes mid-way.
takeaways: Modes: "w" write, "r" read, "a" append. "w" erases existing content!
with open(...) as f: auto-closes the file — the safe pattern.
f.write() saves text; f.read() loads it all back.
lessons.code:
# Write
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Learn. Build. Shine.\n")
    f.write("Day 1: Python basics\n")

# Read it back
with open("notes.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()

print(content)
print("Lines:", content.strip().split("\n"))

quiz.q: Which mode appends to a file without erasing it?
quiz.why: "a" = append. "w" would wipe the file first!

quiz.q: Why is with open(...) preferred?
quiz.why: The with block guarantees the file is closed, even on errors.

quiz.q: What prints? Write "ab" to f.txt with "w", then read it back and print it.
quiz.why: Write mode saves "ab", then read mode loads it back.

quiz.q: A file holds "hi". After with open("f.txt", "a") as f: f.write("!"), it holds…
quiz.why: Append mode adds to the end without erasing.

quiz.q: What does f.readline() return?
quiz.why: readline() reads up to and including the next newline.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank to open a file for writing:
challenge.code:
with open("data.txt", ___) as f:
    f.write("hi")
challenge.hint: The write mode is a single letter…

lessons.title: List Comprehensions
lessons.explain: List comprehensions compress a loop-and-collect pattern into a single readable line — once it clicks, you will use them everywhere. The syntax reads almost like English: transform each item, for each item, optionally only if some condition holds. They are not just shorter; they are usually faster than the equivalent loop.
takeaways: [expr for item in items] transforms every item into a new list.
Add "if cond" at the end to keep only matching items.
Comprehensions beat manual append-loops for clarity and speed.
lessons.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
squares = [n * n for n in nums]
print(squares)
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
print(evens)

quiz.q: What does [n * n for n in nums] build?
options: A list of each number squared
quiz.why: The expression n * n is evaluated for every n, collecting the results.

quiz.q: In [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0], what does the if do?
quiz.why: The trailing if filters: only items passing the test are included.

quiz.q: What is [n if n % 2 == 0 else -n for n in range(4)]?
quiz.why: The conditional expression picks n for evens and -n for odds.

quiz.q: Which comprehension collects only the words longer than 3 letters?
options: [w for w in words if len(w) > 3]
[w for w in words if w > 3]
[w if len(w) > 3 for w in words]
quiz.why: The filter if goes after the for, and len(w) > 3 tests the length.

quiz.q: Compared to an append-loop, a comprehension is usually…
quiz.why: Comprehensions are optimized and read as one idea.

challenge.code:
words = ["hi", "hello", "hey"]
long = [w for w in words if len(w) > 2]
print(long)
challenge.hint: Check the length of each word — which are longer than 2 letters?

lessons.title: Error Handling
lessons.explain: Real programs hit real problems: missing files, bad input, network hiccups. try/except lets your code handle failure gracefully instead of crashing. else runs when nothing went wrong, and finally always runs — perfect for cleanup.
takeaways: Put risky code in try and the recovery plan in except.
Match specific exceptions (ValueError) before broad ones.
finally always runs — use it for cleanup like closing files.
lessons.code:
try:
    age = int("twenty")
except ValueError:
    print("That is not a number")
    age = 0
finally:
    print("Done, age =", age)

quiz.q: When does the except block run?
options: Only when an error occurs in try
Only when there is no error
quiz.why: except runs only if the try block raises a matching exception.

quiz.q: What does finally guarantee?
options: Its code runs whether or not an error happened
quiz.why: finally executes no matter how the try block exits.

quiz.q: What does this print? try: x = 1/1, except ZeroDivisionError: x = 0, print(x)
quiz.why: No error occurs, so the except block is skipped.

quiz.q: Why put except ValueError before except Exception?
options: Specific handlers must come first or they are never reached
quiz.why: Exception would catch everything first, hiding the specific handler.

quiz.q: What prints? try: raise ValueError("bad"), except ValueError: print("caught")
quiz.why: raise triggers the matching except block.

challenge.hint: Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError, which is caught.

lessons.title: File Handling
lessons.explain: Programs become far more useful when they can save and load data, and files are the simplest way. The with statement opens a file and guarantees it gets closed, even if something goes wrong. Learn the read/write modes once and you will reuse this pattern for logs, configs, and datasets.
takeaways: with open(path) as f: auto-closes the file, even on errors.
'w' overwrites, 'a' appends, 'r' (the default) reads.
f.read() grabs everything; f.readline() grabs one line.
lessons.code:
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Python is fun\n")

with open("notes.txt") as f:
    text = f.read()
print(text)

quiz.q: Why use "with open(...) as f:"?
quiz.why: with guarantees the file closes when the block exits, even on errors.

quiz.q: What does open("notes.txt", "w") do if the file exists?
quiz.why: Write mode truncates the file; use "a" to append instead.

quiz.q: What does this print? Write "line1\nline2\n" to t.txt, reopen it, print(f.readline().strip())
quiz.why: readline() grabs just the first line.

quiz.q: Reading a file that does not exist raises…
quiz.why: Read mode requires the file to already exist.

quiz.q: What is the risk of open() without with or close()?
options: The file may stay open and data may not flush
quiz.why: Unclosed files can lose buffered data and leak resources.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank to read the whole file as a string:
challenge.code:
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    text = f.____()
print(text)
challenge.hint: The method that reads everything at once.

lessons.title: OOP Basics
lessons.explain: Classes let you bundle data and the functions that work on it into one tidy package — a Dog knows its name and how to bark. __init__ sets up each new object, and self is how methods refer to the specific instance they are working on. OOP is how large Python programs stay organized.
takeaways: class defines the blueprint; calling it creates an instance.
__init__ runs at creation time and sets up the object's data.
self is the instance — always the first parameter of a method.

quiz.q: What is self in a method?
options: The instance the method was called on
quiz.why: self refers to the particular object the method is operating on.

quiz.q: When does __init__ run?
quiz.why: __init__ is the constructor — it runs each time you instantiate the class.

quiz.q: What does this print? class Dog with __init__(self, name) and bark() returning self.name + " says woof", then rex = Dog("Rex"), print(rex.bark())
quiz.why: bark() combines self.name with the string.

quiz.q: After d1 = Dog("A") and d2 = Dog("B"), d1.name is…
quiz.why: Each instance keeps its own data.

quiz.q: A method defined as def speak(): with no self fails when called because…
options: Python passes the instance automatically, so self is required
quiz.why: The instance is always passed as the first argument.

challenge.hint: __init__ stores the argument on the new instance.

lessons.title: Modules & Imports
lessons.explain: You do not have to write everything yourself — Python ships with a huge standard library. import brings in a whole module, while from...import grabs just what you need. math, random, and datetime cover an enormous amount of everyday work.
takeaways: import math loads the module; math.sqrt(16) uses it.
from random import choice grabs just one function.
Standard library first: check math, random, datetime before writing your own.
lessons.code:
import math
import random

print(math.sqrt(16))
print(math.pi)
lucky = random.choice(["Asha", "Ravi", "Mina"])
print("Winner:", lucky)

quiz.q: What does "import math" give you?
options: Access to math functions like sqrt
quiz.why: Importing a module makes all its functions and constants available.

quiz.q: How do you import only choice from random?
quiz.why: from X import Y pulls a single name out of a module.

quiz.q: What does this print? import math, print(math.sqrt(16))
quiz.why: sqrt(16) is 4.0 — math functions return floats.

quiz.q: After import datetime, today's date comes from…
quiz.why: You go through the module name: datetime.date.today().

quiz.q: What does this print? from math import pi, print(round(pi, 2))
quiz.why: round(pi, 2) keeps two decimal places.

challenge.code:
import math
print(math.floor(3.9))
challenge.hint: floor() rounds down to the nearest whole number.

lessons.title: Lambda, map, filter
lessons.explain: Sometimes a full def is overkill — lambda creates a tiny throwaway function right where you need it. map applies a function to every item, filter keeps only the items that pass a test, and sorted with a key function sorts by anything you can compute. Together they are a compact toolkit for transforming data.
takeaways: lambda n: n * 2 is a tiny function with no name.
map(f, items) transforms; filter(f, items) keeps matches.
sorted(items, key=...) sorts by whatever the key function returns.
lessons.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
doubled = list(map(lambda n: n * 2, nums))
print(doubled)
evens = list(filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, nums))
print(evens)

quiz.q: What is a lambda?
quiz.why: lambda defines a small function inline without a name.

quiz.q: What does map do?
options: Applies a function to every item
quiz.why: map runs the given function on each item and yields the results.

quiz.q: What is list(filter(lambda n: n > 2, [1, 2, 3, 4]))?
quiz.why: filter keeps only the items where the test is True.

quiz.q: What is sorted([3, 1, 2], key=lambda x: -x)?
quiz.why: Sorting by -x puts the largest value first.

quiz.q: Can a lambda body have multiple statements?
options: Yes, as many as you like
quiz.why: A lambda body must be a single expression.

challenge.code:
nums = [5, 2, 8]
print(sorted(nums, key=lambda n: -n))
challenge.hint: Sorting by -n puts the biggest number first.

lessons.title: *args & **kwargs
lessons.explain: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. Together they make flexible functions that accept any number of arguments.
takeaways: *args gathers extra positional args into a tuple.
**kwargs gathers extra keyword args into a dict.
Use *args/**kwargs to forward arguments to other functions.

quiz.q: What type does *args collect arguments into?
quiz.why: *args always packs extra positional arguments into a tuple.

quiz.q: In def f(a, *args, **kwargs):, where do extra keyword arguments go?
quiz.why: **kwargs collects any extra keyword arguments into a dictionary.

quiz.q: What does f(*[1, 2]) do when calling f(a, b)?
options: Passes the list as one argument
Unpacks the list into a and b
quiz.why: The * in a call unpacks an iterable into separate positional arguments.

challenge.hint: join() glues the tuple items with the separator string.

lessons.title: Advanced String Formatting
lessons.explain: Beyond basic f-strings, Python's format mini-language lets you control width, alignment, padding, and decimal places. It turns raw numbers into clean, readable output.
takeaways: f'{x:>10}' right-aligns; f'{x:<10}' left-aligns; f'{x:^10}' centers.
f'{pi:.2f}' rounds a float to 2 decimal places.
f'{n:,}' adds thousands separators; f'{n:05d}' zero-pads.
lessons.code:
pi = 3.14159
n = 1234567
word = "hi"

print(f"{pi:.2f}")
print(f"{n:,}")
print(f"{word:>10}|")
print(f"{42:05d}")

quiz.q: What does f"{3.14159:.2f}" produce?
quiz.why: .2f rounds to two decimal places, so 3.14159 becomes 3.14.

quiz.q: What does f"{7:04d}" print?
quiz.why: 04d means pad with zeros to width 4.

quiz.q: What does f"{1000000:,}" print?
quiz.why: The , format spec adds thousands separators.

challenge.code:
score = 9.5
print(f"Score: {score:>6.1f}")
challenge.hint: Width 6 with one decimal — count the characters.

lessons.title: enumerate, zip & Unpacking in Loops
lessons.explain: enumerate() gives you index + item as you loop, zip() pairs up two lists, and unpacking splits each pair into named variables. Together they replace most manual index juggling.
takeaways: for i, x in enumerate(items) gives index and value together.
zip(a, b) pairs items from two lists, stopping at the shorter one.
Unpacking like for name, score in pairs: keeps loops readable.

quiz.q: What does enumerate(['a','b']) yield?
quiz.why: enumerate pairs each item with its index, starting at 0 by default.

quiz.q: zip([1,2,3], ['a','b']) produces how many pairs?
quiz.why: zip stops at the shorter iterable, so you get 2 pairs.

quiz.q: What does a, b = (10, 20) do?
options: Assigns 10 to a and 20 to b
quiz.why: Tuple unpacking splits the values into the named variables.

challenge.hint: Unpack each pair, then string * number repeats the string.

lessons.title: Dict & Set Comprehensions
lessons.explain: Just like list comprehensions, you can build dicts and sets in one line with {k: v for ...} and {x for ...}. They are the fastest way to transform mappings and collections.
takeaways: {k: v for k, v in pairs} builds a dict in one line.
{x for x in items} builds a set, dropping duplicates automatically.
Add if to filter: {k: v for k, v in d.items() if v > 0}.

quiz.q: What does {x: x**2 for x in range(3)} create?
quiz.why: The k: v form builds a dict mapping each x to its square.

quiz.q: What does {c for c in 'aab'} evaluate to?
quiz.why: Set comprehensions drop duplicates, leaving one 'a' and one 'b'.

quiz.q: Which filters a dict comprehension to positive values?
options: {k: v for k, v in d.items() if v > 0}
{k: v if v > 0 for k, v in d.items()}
quiz.why: The if filter goes at the end of the comprehension, after the for clause.

challenge.code:
nums = [1, 2, 2, 3]
print({n * 10 for n in nums})
challenge.hint: Sets keep only one copy of each value.

lessons.title: Sorting with key Functions
lessons.explain: sorted() and list.sort() accept a key function that computes the value to sort by. Combined with lambda or str.lower, you can sort by length, last name, or anything you define.
takeaways: key=len sorts strings by length instead of alphabetically.
key=str.lower sorts case-insensitively.
reverse=True flips the order; sort() is stable so ties keep original order.
lessons.code:
words = ["pear", "fig", "banana", "kiwi"]

print(sorted(words))
print(sorted(words, key=len))
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower, reverse=True))

quiz.q: What does sorted(['bb', 'a', 'ccc'], key=len) return?
quiz.why: key=len sorts by string length: 1, 2, 3.

quiz.q: How do you sort numbers from largest to smallest?
quiz.why: reverse=True flips the sort direction.

quiz.q: What does key do in sorted()?
options: Computes the value each item is compared by
Limits how many items are sorted
quiz.why: Each item is transformed by key, and sorting compares those results.

challenge.code:
data = [("b", 2), ("a", 3), ("c", 1)]
print(sorted(data, key=lambda t: t[1]))
challenge.hint: The lambda picks the second element of each tuple as the sort key.

lessons.title: Copy vs Deep Copy: The Mutation Trap
lessons.explain: Assigning a list copies the reference, not the data — and even list.copy() only copies the outer layer. Nested lists still share memory unless you use copy.deepcopy().
takeaways: b = a makes both names point to the same list.
a.copy() / list(a) copy only the outer list; nested lists stay shared.
copy.deepcopy(a) clones everything, including nested objects.
lessons.code:
import copy

a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = a.copy()
c = copy.deepcopy(a)

b[0].append(99)
print(a[0])
print(c[0])

quiz.q: After b = a (both lists), b.append(5) does what to a?
quiz.why: b = a copies the reference, so both names share one list.

quiz.q: a = [[1]]; b = a.copy(); b[0].append(2). What is a now?
quiz.why: copy() is shallow: the inner list is still shared, so the change shows up in a.

quiz.q: Which fully clones nested structures?
quiz.why: Only deepcopy recursively clones every nested object.

challenge.code:
import copy

a = [1, [2]]
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
b[1].append(3)
print(a)
print(b)
challenge.hint: deepcopy gives b its own independent inner list.

lessons.title: Exception Hierarchy & Custom Exceptions
lessons.explain: All exceptions inherit from BaseException, and your own error types just subclass Exception. Raising a custom exception makes your code's failures self-documenting.
takeaways: Every built-in error (ValueError, TypeError...) inherits from Exception.
class MyError(Exception): pass creates your own exception type.
Catch specific exceptions; bare except: hides bugs.

quiz.q: What should a custom exception inherit from?
quiz.why: Subclassing Exception plugs your error into Python's normal exception handling.

quiz.q: Why avoid a bare except: ?
options: It also catches real bugs and things like KeyboardInterrupt
quiz.why: A bare except swallows everything, including bugs you actually want to see.

quiz.q: What is the parent of ValueError?
quiz.why: All normal errors derive from Exception, which derives from BaseException.

challenge.hint: A custom exception IS an Exception, so except Exception catches it.

lessons.title: Raising Exceptions & Assertions
lessons.explain: raise lets you signal errors deliberately, and assert states assumptions that should never be false. Both turn silent wrongness into loud, debuggable failures.
takeaways: raise ValueError('msg') throws an error with your message.
assert x > 0, 'msg' crashes if the condition is False.
Use raise for bad input; assert for impossible internal states.

quiz.q: What happens when assert 2 + 2 == 5 runs?
quiz.why: A failed assert raises AssertionError immediately.

quiz.q: When should you use raise instead of assert?
quiz.why: raise is for expected runtime errors like bad input; asserts can be disabled with -O.

quiz.q: What does raise ValueError('bad') do?
quiz.why: raise stops execution and throws the exception with your message.

challenge.code:
def check(n):
    assert n >= 0, "negative!"
    return n * 2

print(check(5))
challenge.hint: 5 >= 0 is True, so the assert passes quietly.

lessons.title: try/except/else/finally: The Full Picture
lessons.explain: else runs only when no exception occurred, and finally runs no matter what — perfect for cleanup. Using all four blocks makes your error handling precise instead of guessy.
takeaways: else: runs only if the try block succeeded — put success code there.
finally: always runs, even on return or uncaught errors.
Keep try blocks small so you know exactly what might fail.

quiz.q: When does the else block of try/except/else run?
options: Only if no exception was raised
Only if an exception was raised
quiz.why: else means 'the try succeeded, so do the success path here'.

quiz.q: When does finally run?
options: Always, even after return or an error
Only if there is no else
quiz.why: finally is guaranteed cleanup — it runs no matter how the try exits.

quiz.q: Why keep try blocks small?
options: So you know exactly which line might fail
Big try blocks are a syntax error
quiz.why: A tiny try block pinpoints the risky operation instead of hiding bugs elsewhere.

challenge.hint: The exception skips else; finally still adds 1 to -1.

lessons.title: Working with CSV Files
lessons.explain: The csv module reads and writes spreadsheet-style data without manual string splitting. These examples use io.StringIO so everything runs without touching your disk.
takeaways: csv.reader turns each row into a list of strings.
csv.DictReader maps rows to dicts using the header row.
Always open real files with newline='' to avoid blank rows.
lessons.code:
import csv, io

text = "name,age\nAl,20\nBo,22\n"
rows = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text)))

for row in rows[1:]:
    print(row[0], "is", row[1])

quiz.q: What does csv.reader yield for each row?
quiz.why: Each row comes back as a list, with every field as a string.

quiz.q: What does csv.DictReader use as dict keys?
quiz.why: DictReader takes the first row as headers and maps every later row to them.

quiz.q: Why open CSV files with newline=''?
options: To stop extra blank rows on some systems
quiz.why: The csv module handles newlines itself; letting Python translate them too creates blank rows.

challenge.code:
import csv, io

text = "a,b\n1,2\n"
rows = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text)))
print(rows[1][0] + rows[1][1])
challenge.hint: CSV fields are strings, so + concatenates them.

lessons.title: JSON: Reading & Writing Data
lessons.explain: JSON is the universal data-exchange format, and Python's json module converts it to dicts and lists in one call. It is how APIs, configs, and saved game states travel.
takeaways: json.loads(text) parses a JSON string into Python objects.
json.dumps(obj) turns dicts/lists back into a JSON string.
JSON keys are always strings; tuples become lists.
lessons.code:
import json

data = {"name": "Al", "scores": [88, 92]}
text = json.dumps(data)
back = json.loads(text)

print(text)
print(back["scores"][0])

quiz.q: json.loads() converts a JSON string into what?
quiz.why: loads parses JSON text into real Python objects like dicts and lists.

quiz.q: Which converts a Python dict to a JSON string?
quiz.why: dumps (dump-string) serializes; loads (load-string) parses.

quiz.q: What happens to the tuple (1, 2) in json.dumps?
quiz.why: JSON has no tuples, so they serialize as arrays.

challenge.code:
import json

s = "{\"x\": [1, 2]}"
d = json.loads(s)
print(d["x"][1] * 10)
challenge.hint: Parse first, then index: d['x'] is [1, 2].

lessons.title: Files & Folders with pathlib
lessons.explain: pathlib treats paths as objects with handy methods instead of fragile string juggling. Path('a') / 'b' joins paths, and .exists(), .mkdir(), .glob() cover everyday file chores.
takeaways: Path('docs') / 'notes.txt' joins paths with /.
.exists(), .is_file(), .mkdir(parents=True) inspect and create.
.glob('*.py') lists matching files in a folder.
lessons.code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("projects") / "demo" / "notes.txt"

print(p.name)
print(p.suffix)
print(p.parent)

quiz.q: What does Path('a') / 'b.txt' produce?
quiz.why: Path overloads / to join path parts cleanly.

quiz.q: Which lists all .py files in a folder?
options: glob lives in the os module only
quiz.why: glob(pattern) yields every path matching the pattern.

quiz.q: What does p.suffix return for Path('a/b.txt')?
quiz.why: suffix is the file extension, including the dot.

challenge.code:
from pathlib import Path

p = Path("data") / "x.csv"
print(p.stem)
print(p.parent.name)
challenge.hint: stem is the name without extension; parent.name is the folder name.

lessons.title: OOP: Inheritance
lessons.explain: Inheritance lets a child class reuse and extend a parent class: the child gets all parent methods for free and can override the ones it wants to change. Use super() to call the parent's version.
takeaways: class Dog(Animal): makes Dog inherit everything from Animal.
Override a method by redefining it in the child class.
super().__init__(...) calls the parent's constructor.

quiz.q: What does class Dog(Animal): mean?
quiz.why: The parent class goes in parentheses after the child class name.

quiz.q: What does super().__init__(name) do in a child class?
quiz.why: super() gives access to the parent so you can reuse its setup code.

quiz.q: If Dog does not define speak(), but Animal does, what happens on d.speak()?
quiz.why: Missing methods are looked up on the parent class automatically.

challenge.hint: super().hi() calls A's version, returning 'A'.

lessons.title: OOP: Encapsulation with @property
lessons.explain: @property lets a method masquerade as an attribute, so you can add validation or computed values later without changing how anyone uses your class. Setters guard what values are allowed in.
takeaways: @property makes a method readable like an attribute: obj.area.
@x.setter validates new values before storing them.
It keeps the simple obj.x API while hiding logic underneath.

quiz.q: How do you read a @property named area on c?
quiz.why: A property is accessed like a plain attribute — the method runs behind the scenes.

quiz.q: What is @x.setter used for?
quiz.why: The setter intercepts assignment so you can reject bad values.

quiz.q: Why use @property instead of a plain attribute?
options: You can add logic/validation later without changing callers
quiz.why: Callers keep writing obj.x while you sneak in computed or guarded behavior.

lessons.title: OOP: Dunder Methods (__str__, __len__, __eq__)
lessons.explain: Dunder (double-underscore) methods let your objects speak Python's native language: __str__ for printing, __len__ for len(), __eq__ for ==. Implement them and your class feels built-in.
takeaways: __str__ controls what print(obj) shows.
__len__ makes len(obj) work.
__eq__ defines what == means for your objects.

quiz.q: Which dunder method controls print(obj)?
quiz.why: Python calls __str__ whenever your object needs a readable string form.

quiz.q: What must __len__ return?
quiz.why: len() expects __len__ to give back a non-negative integer.

quiz.q: Without __eq__, what does == compare for objects?
quiz.why: The default == only checks whether both names point to the very same object.

challenge.hint: __eq__ compares the .v values, not object identity.

lessons.title: OOP: Class vs Instance, @classmethod & @staticmethod
lessons.explain: Instance methods work on one object (self); class methods work on the class itself (cls) and make great alternate constructors; static methods are plain functions that just live in the class namespace.
takeaways: Instance attributes live on self; class attributes are shared by all instances.
@classmethod takes cls — use it for alternate constructors like from_string().
@staticmethod takes neither self nor cls — just namespaced helper logic.

quiz.q: What is the first parameter of a @classmethod?
quiz.why: Class methods receive the class itself as cls, not an instance.

quiz.q: Where is a class attribute like count stored?
options: On the class, shared by all instances
quiz.why: Class attributes live on the class object, so every instance sees the same one.

quiz.q: When is @staticmethod the right choice?
options: A helper that needs neither self nor cls
quiz.why: Static methods are just logically-grouped functions with no access to instance or class state.

challenge.hint: Static methods can be called straight on the class.

lessons.title: Iterators & the Iterator Protocol
lessons.explain: An iterator is an object with __next__() that hands out one item at a time; iter() gets one from any iterable. for loops are just pretty wrappers around this protocol.
takeaways: iter([1, 2]) returns an iterator; next(it) pulls the next item.
When items run out, next() raises StopIteration.
Custom classes become iterable by defining __iter__ and __next__.
lessons.code:
it = iter(["a", "b"])

print(next(it))
print(next(it))

for x in [10, 20]:
    print(x)

quiz.q: What does next(it) do when the iterator is exhausted?
quiz.why: StopIteration is the signal that there are no more items — for loops catch it silently.

quiz.q: What does iter([1, 2, 3]) return?
quiz.why: iter() builds a fresh iterator object that tracks position separately from the list.

quiz.q: Which two methods make a custom iterator?
quiz.why: __iter__ returns the iterator and __next__ produces each item — that is the protocol.

challenge.code:
it = iter([5, 6])
first = next(it)
rest = list(it)
print(first)
print(rest)
challenge.hint: The first next() consumes 5, so list() only sees what is left.

lessons.title: Generator Expressions & itertools
lessons.explain: Generator expressions (x*2 for x in data) compute values lazily, one at a time — perfect for huge sequences. itertools adds pro tools like count(), cycle(), and chain() for combining iterables.
takeaways: (x*x for x in range(10**9)) uses almost no memory — values are made on demand.
itertools.count(5) is an infinite counter; pair with islice to take a few.
itertools.chain(a, b) loops over a then b as one stream.
lessons.code:
import itertools

gen = (x * x for x in range(5))
print(list(gen))

combo = itertools.chain("ab", [1, 2])
print(list(combo))

quiz.q: How is (x for x in data) different from [x for x in data]?
options: It is lazy — values are produced one at a time
It is faster for small lists
quiz.why: Parentheses make a generator: nothing is computed until you iterate.

quiz.q: What does itertools.chain('ab', [1]) yield?
quiz.why: chain flattens its arguments into one continuous stream of items.

quiz.q: Why use a generator for 10**9 items?
options: It never stores them all in memory
quiz.why: A generator holds only its current state, so memory stays tiny no matter the size.

challenge.code:
import itertools

c = itertools.count(10)
print([next(c) for _ in range(3)])
challenge.hint: count(10) starts at 10 and steps by 1.

lessons.title: Recursion Patterns & Limits
lessons.explain: Recursion solves a problem by solving smaller copies of itself, with a base case that stops the descent. Python caps the call stack (~1000 frames), so deep recursion needs a loop instead.
takeaways: Every recursive function needs a base case, or it recurses forever.
Trace small inputs by hand: f(3) → f(2) → f(1) → base.
Python's default recursion limit is 1000 — deep recursion raises RecursionError.

quiz.q: What happens without a base case?
quiz.why: Python's call stack has a limit; endless recursion hits RecursionError.

quiz.q: What does countdown(3) print first?
quiz.why: It prints n before recursing, so 3 comes out first.

quiz.q: How deep can Python recurse by default?
quiz.why: sys.getrecursionlimit() defaults to 1000 to protect the C stack.

challenge.hint: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 — it sums down to the base case.

lessons.title: Closures & Higher-Order Functions
lessons.explain: A closure is a function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created. Functions that take or return other functions — like decorators do — are called higher-order functions.
takeaways: An inner function keeps access to its enclosing function's variables.
return inner (no parens) hands back the function itself.
Higher-order functions take functions as args or return them.
lessons.code:
def make_adder(n):
    def adder(x):
        return x + n
    return adder

add5 = make_adder(5)
print(add5(10))
print(add5(20))

quiz.q: What does make_adder(5) return?
options: A function that adds 5 to its argument
quiz.why: It returns the inner adder function, which still remembers n=5.

quiz.q: What makes adder a closure?
options: It remembers n from make_adder's scope
quiz.why: A closure captures variables from its enclosing scope even after that scope exits.

quiz.q: What is a higher-order function?
options: One that takes or returns functions
quiz.why: Treating functions as values — passing or returning them — is the definition.

challenge.hint: square remembers exp=2, so it computes 6**2.

lessons.title: Big-O Intuition & Timing Code
lessons.explain: Big-O describes how runtime grows as input grows: O(1) stays flat, O(n) grows linearly, O(n²) explodes. time.perf_counter() lets you measure the difference yourself.
takeaways: O(1): constant — dict lookup. O(n): loop once. O(n²): loop inside a loop.
Doubling n doubles O(n) time but quadruples O(n²) time.
Use time.perf_counter() around code to measure real seconds.
lessons.code:
import time

start = time.perf_counter()
total = sum(range(10**6))
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start

print(total)
print(round(elapsed, 3), "seconds")

quiz.q: A double loop over n items is which complexity?
quiz.why: n iterations × n inner iterations = n² total steps.

quiz.q: If O(n²) code takes 1s for n=1000, roughly how long for n=2000?
quiz.why: Doubling n quadruples n² work: 2² = 4.

quiz.q: Which is O(1)?
quiz.why: Hash lookup takes the same time regardless of dict size.

challenge.code:
import time

t0 = time.perf_counter()
s = 0
for i in range(1000):
    s += i
t1 = time.perf_counter()
print(s)
print((t1 - t0) >= 0)
challenge.hint: Sum of 0..999 is 499500; elapsed time is always >= 0.

lessons.title: Regular Expressions Basics
lessons.explain: Regular expressions are mini-patterns for finding text: \d matches digits, + means 'one or more', and re.findall() pulls out every match. One line of regex replaces paragraphs of string-splitting code.
takeaways: re.findall(r'\d+', s) extracts all number chunks from s.
\d = digit, \w = word char, . = any char, + = one-or-more.
Use raw strings r'...' so backslashes stay intact.
lessons.code:
import re

s = "Call 555-1234 or 555-9999"
nums = re.findall(r"\d+", s)

print(nums)
print(re.sub(r"\d", "#", "abc123"))

quiz.q: What does re.findall(r'\d+', 'a12b3') return?
quiz.why: + grabs one-or-more digits together, so '12' is one match.

quiz.q: Why use raw strings r'...' for regex?
options: So \d stays a backslash-d, not an escape
quiz.why: Without r'', Python would turn \d into an escape before regex sees it.

quiz.q: What does re.sub(r'\d', '#', 'a1b2') produce?
quiz.why: sub replaces every single digit with #, leaving letters alone.

challenge.code:
import re

text = "hi there!"
words = re.findall(r"\w+", text)
print(words)
challenge.hint: \w+ matches runs of word characters — punctuation splits them.

lessons.title: Capstone: File Organizer Script
lessons.explain: Time to combine everything: this script scans a folder and sorts files into subfolders by extension. It uses pathlib, dicts, loops, and functions — the full intermediate toolkit in one real program.
takeaways: pathlib's .suffix and .iterdir() make file scanning painless.
A dict mapping extensions → folder names drives the whole sort.
mkdir(exist_ok=True) safely creates folders that may already exist.

quiz.q: What does Path(folder).iterdir() yield?
quiz.why: iterdir() iterates over every entry directly inside the folder.

quiz.q: Why mkdir(exist_ok=True)?
options: It will not crash if the folder already exists
quiz.why: exist_ok=True makes repeat runs safe instead of raising FileExistsError.

quiz.q: How does the script decide where a file goes?
options: Looks up its .suffix in the mapping dict
quiz.why: The mapping dict pairs each extension with its destination folder name.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank so photos (.jpg) go to the 'images' folder.
challenge.code:
mapping = {____: "images"}
print(mapping[".jpg"])  # prints images
challenge.hint: The key must match f.suffix for a photo file.

lessons.title: List Comprehensions & Lambdas
lessons.explain: Comprehensions build lists in one expressive line — [expr for x in items if cond]. They're faster to read and often faster to run than manual loops. Lambdas are tiny anonymous functions, perfect for short transformations you pass to sorted(), map() or filter().
takeaways: [x**2 for x in range(5)] builds a list in a single line.
Add if to filter: [x for x in items if x > 0].
lambda args: expr creates a throwaway one-line function.
lessons.code:
squares = [x**2 for x in range(1, 11)]
print("Squares:", squares)

evens = [x for x in range(20) if x % 2 == 0]
print("Evens:", evens)

nums = [5, 2, 9, 1]
print("Sorted desc:", sorted(nums, key=lambda x: -x))

quiz.q: [x**2 for x in range(3)] equals…
quiz.why: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2 — and their squares are 0, 1, 4.

quiz.q: A lambda is…
quiz.why: lambda creates a small anonymous function, e.g. lambda x: x * 2.

quiz.q: What is "-".join([str(n) for n in range(3)])?
quiz.why: The comprehension makes ['0','1','2'], then join glues them with '-'.

quiz.q: sorted(['bb', 'a', 'ccc'], key=len) gives…
quiz.why: key=len sorts by length: 1, 2, 3.

quiz.q: What is (lambda x: x * 3)(4)?
quiz.why: The lambda is called immediately with 4.

challenge.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print([n * 2 for n in nums if n % 2 == 0])
challenge.hint: Filter keeps 2 and 4, then doubles each → [4, 8].

lessons.title: Generators & yield
lessons.explain: Generators produce values lazily — one at a time, using almost no memory. yield pauses the function, hands out a value, and resumes where it left off when asked for the next one. Perfect for huge or infinite sequences that would never fit in a list.
takeaways: yield turns a function into a generator that produces values on demand.
Generators are memory-efficient: items are made one at a time.
(expr for x in items) is a generator expression — like a comprehension but lazy.
lessons.code:
def fibonacci(n):
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        yield a
        a, b = b, a + b

print(list(fibonacci(10)))

# Memory-friendly: squares of 1M numbers, one at a time
gen = (x**2 for x in range(1_000_000))
print("First 3:", [next(gen) for _ in range(3)])

quiz.q: What does yield do?
