quiz.why: yield hands out a value and freezes the function's state until the next value is requested.

quiz.q: Why use a generator for a million items?
quiz.why: Items are produced one at a time instead of building a giant list in memory.

quiz.q: What does this print? def g(): yield 1, yield 2, then print(list(g()))
quiz.why: list() pulls both yielded values out of the generator.

quiz.q: What does next() do to a generator?
options: Resumes it until the next yield
quiz.why: Each next() continues execution from after the last yield.

quiz.q: Why does the second list(gen) print []? gen = (x for x in range(3)), print(list(gen)), print(list(gen))
quiz.why: A generator cannot be rewound; once consumed, it stays done.

challenge.code:
def gen():
    yield 1
    yield 2
g = gen()
print(next(g))
challenge.hint: next() resumes the generator up to the first yield → 1.

lessons.title: Decorators
lessons.explain: Decorators wrap functions to add behaviour — timing, logging, caching, access control — without touching the function's own code. The @ syntax applies a decorator cleanly. Under the hood, @timer on f is just f = timer(f).
takeaways: @decorator above def applies wrapper logic around the function.
The wrapper uses *args, **kwargs to accept any arguments.
@wraps(func) preserves the original function's name and docstring.

quiz.q: What does @timer above def slow_add do?
options: Wraps it to add timing behaviour
quiz.why: The decorator replaces slow_add with wrapper, which times the call then returns the result.

quiz.q: Why use @wraps(func) inside a decorator?
quiz.why: Without it, the wrapped function would report the wrapper's name instead of the original.

quiz.q: With the lesson's @shout decorator, greet() returns…
quiz.why: wrapper() returns func().upper().

quiz.q: When is shout(greet) actually applied?
quiz.why: Decoration happens once, at function definition time.

quiz.q: A decorator whose outer function forgets return wrapper causes…
options: TypeError when calling the decorated function
quiz.why: The name gets bound to None instead of a function.

challenge.hint: @shout replaces greet with wrapper, which uppercases the result.

lessons.title: Modules, pip & Virtual Environments
lessons.explain: Modules organise code into importable files. pip installs third-party packages from PyPI. Virtual environments (venv) give each project its own isolated set of packages so versions never clash. This trio is the professional Python workflow — learn it now and every future project gets easier.
takeaways: import brings in stdlib or third-party modules; pip installs them.
python -m venv venv creates an isolated environment per project.
pip freeze > requirements.txt locks exact versions for sharing.
lessons.code:
# mymath.py  →  import mymath
# def square(x): return x * x

# In your terminal:
#   python -m venv venv        # create isolated environment
#   source venv/bin/activate   # activate it
#   pip install requests       # install a package
#   pip freeze > requirements.txt   # lock dependencies

import math, random
print("π ≈", round(math.pi, 4))
print("Lucky number:", random.randint(1, 100))

quiz.q: What does pip install requests do?
quiz.why: pip is Python's package installer; it fetches packages from PyPI.

quiz.q: Why use a virtual environment?
quiz.why: Each project gets its own package versions — no conflicts between projects.

quiz.q: What does this print? import math, print(math.floor(3.9))
quiz.why: floor() rounds down to 3.

quiz.q: What does pip freeze > requirements.txt do?
options: Saves the exact installed package versions
quiz.why: It records precise versions so others can recreate the environment.

quiz.q: After import random, how do you call randint?
quiz.why: Names live under the module namespace.

challenge.prompt: Fill the blank to create a virtual environment named venv:
challenge.code: python -m ___ venv
challenge.hint: The stdlib module for virtual environments is called venv.

lessons.title: Context Managers & the with Statement
lessons.explain: You've already used with open(...) — but with works with any context manager, guaranteeing setup and cleanup even when errors strike. Files close, locks release, timers stop. You can build your own with a class defining __enter__/__exit__, or more simply with the @contextmanager decorator: code before yield runs on entry, code after yield runs on exit.
takeaways: with guarantees cleanup (close, release, rollback) even on errors.
@contextmanager: code before yield = setup, after yield = teardown.
Use them for files, locks, timers, database transactions.
lessons.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager
import time

@contextmanager
def stopwatch(label):
    start = time.time()
    print(f"START {label}...")
    try:
        yield  # your code runs here
    finally:
        print(f"DONE {label} in {time.time()-start:.2f}s")

with stopwatch("data crunch"):
    total = sum(range(100000))
    print("total =", total)

quiz.q: What does a context manager guarantee?
options: Cleanup runs even if errors occur
quiz.why: That's the whole point of with — reliable teardown no matter what.

quiz.q: In a @contextmanager function, code after yield runs…
quiz.why: yield splits the function: before = setup, after = teardown on exit.

quiz.q: In the lesson's stopwatch example, when does "DONE …" print?
quiz.why: Code after yield runs when the with block exits.

quiz.q: Which two methods define a class-based context manager?
quiz.why: Python calls __enter__ on entry and __exit__ on exit.

quiz.q: Which @contextmanager pattern is correct?
quiz.why: Code before yield sets up; code after yield tears down.

challenge.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager
@contextmanager
def tag(name):
    print(f"<{name}>")
    yield
    print(f"</{name}>")

with tag("b"):
    print("hi")
challenge.hint: Entry prints , the body prints hi, exit prints .

lessons.title: Decorators
lessons.explain: A decorator is a function that wraps another function to add behavior — logging, timing, access checks — without touching its code. The @ syntax is just shorthand for passing your function through the decorator. Once you see the pattern, you will spot decorators everywhere in real Python projects.
takeaways: @decorator above def is shorthand for func = decorator(func).
The wrapper function runs extra code before/after the original.
Decorators keep cross-cutting concerns (timing, logging) out of business logic.

quiz.q: What does @shout above "def greet" do?
options: Passes greet through the shout decorator
quiz.why: @shout is shorthand for greet = shout(greet).

quiz.q: What must a decorator return?
quiz.why: The decorator returns the replacement function that gets called instead.

quiz.q: What does this print? def shout(func): def wrapper(): return func().upper(), return wrapper, then @shout, def greet(): return "hello", print(greet())
quiz.why: wrapper() returns func().upper().

quiz.q: With @a above @b above def f, which decorator applies first?
quiz.why: Decorators apply bottom-up: f = a(b(f)).

quiz.q: Why should the wrapper accept *args, **kwargs?
options: So it works with any arguments
quiz.why: The wrapper must forward whatever arguments the wrapped function takes.

challenge.hint: The wrapper adds one star on each side of the result.

lessons.title: Generators & Iterators
lessons.explain: Generators produce values one at a time, pausing at each yield and resuming on demand. That laziness means you can work with huge or even infinite sequences without building them all in memory. for loops and next() both know how to pull values from a generator.
takeaways: yield pauses a function and emits one value; next() resumes it.
Generators are lazy — values are produced only when asked for.
A generator is single-use: once exhausted, it stays exhausted.

quiz.q: How is yield different from return?
options: It pauses the function and resumes later, producing a sequence
quiz.why: yield suspends the function state; the next call continues after it.

quiz.q: Why are generators memory-friendly?
options: They produce one item at a time instead of building a whole list
quiz.why: Laziness means only one value exists in memory at a time.

quiz.q: What does this print? def c(n): while n > 0: yield n, n -= 1, then print(list(c(3)))
quiz.why: It yields 3, then 2, then 1.

quiz.q: What does for x in countdown(3): do with the generator?
options: Pulls values one by one until exhausted
quiz.why: for keeps calling next() until StopIteration.

quiz.q: Calling next() on an exhausted generator raises…
quiz.why: Exhaustion is signaled with StopIteration.

challenge.code:
def gen():
    yield 1
    yield 2
g = gen()
print(next(g))
print(next(g))
challenge.hint: Each next() call resumes where the generator paused.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.explain: Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of it. Every recursive function needs a base case — the simple situation where it stops calling itself. It is elegant for problems like factorial or tree traversal, but always respect Python's recursion limit.
takeaways: A recursive function calls itself with a smaller input.
The base case stops the recursion — without it, you recurse forever.
Each call waits for the deeper one, so deep recursion uses lots of stack.

quiz.q: What is a base case?
options: The condition that stops the recursion
quiz.why: The base case is the terminating condition every recursion needs.

quiz.q: What happens without a base case?
options: Infinite recursion until Python stops it
quiz.why: The calls never stop until Python hits the recursion limit and raises.

quiz.q: What is factorial(4)?
While computing factorial(4), how many factorial calls are waiting at the deepest point?
quiz.why: The calls for 4, 3, 2 and 1 are all stacked up.

quiz.q: What does this print? def s(n): if n == 0: return 0, return n + s(n-1), then print(s(4))

challenge.hint: Each call prints, then recurses with n - 1 — until 0 stops it silently.

lessons.title: Sorting & Searching
lessons.explain: Sorting puts data in order so searching becomes dramatically cheaper. Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted list, finding any item in about log2(n) steps — roughly 20 steps for a million items. Python's own sort is world-class, so learn the intuition and reach for the built-ins.
takeaways: Sorting once makes every later search cheap.
Binary search halves the search space each step: O(log n).
Use list.sort()/sorted() and the bisect module instead of hand-rolling.
lessons.code:
import bisect
nums = [1, 2, 5, 8]
i = bisect.bisect_left(nums, 5)
print("index:", i)
print("sorted:", sorted([5, 2, 8, 1]))

quiz.q: Why must data be sorted for binary search?
options: Each comparison can eliminate half the remaining items
Python requires it for all searches
quiz.why: Only sorted order lets one comparison discard half the candidates.

quiz.q: Roughly how many steps does binary search need for 1,000,000 sorted items?
quiz.why: log2(1,000,000) is about 20 — that is the power of halving.

quiz.q: What does this print? import bisect, nums = [1, 2, 5, 8], print(bisect.bisect_left(nums, 5))
quiz.why: 5 sits at index 2 in the sorted list.

quiz.q: Binary search runs in…
quiz.why: Halving the search space each step gives logarithmic time.

quiz.q: What is sorted([5, 2, 8, 1])?
quiz.why: sorted() returns a new ascending list.

challenge.code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
nums.sort()
print(nums[0])
challenge.hint: sort() arranges the list from smallest to largest.

lessons.title: Dictionaries in Depth
lessons.explain: Dictionaries reward deeper study: .get() with a default makes counting patterns trivial, .items() lets you loop over keys and values together, and dict comprehensions build mappings in one line. These three idioms show up constantly in real-world Python.
takeaways: counts[k] = counts.get(k, 0) + 1 is the classic counting idiom.
.items() loops over (key, value) pairs together.
{k: v for ...} builds dicts as compactly as list comprehensions build lists.

quiz.q: What does counts.get(v, 0) do here?
options: Returns the current count, or 0 if the key is new
quiz.why: The default 0 handles first-time keys without a KeyError.

quiz.q: What does {n: n * n for n in range(4)} create?
options: A dict mapping 0-3 to their squares
quiz.why: The k: v form in a comprehension builds a dictionary.

quiz.q: In the lesson's vote counter, counts["a"] is…
quiz.why: "a" appears three times in the votes list.

quiz.q: In for k, v in d.items():, k and v are…
options: The key and value of each pair
quiz.why: .items() yields (key, value) tuples.

quiz.q: What is {w: len(w) for w in ["a", "bb", "ccc"] if len(w) > 1}?
quiz.why: "a" is filtered out, leaving bb mapped to 2 and ccc to 3.

challenge.hint: get returns 1, then 10 is added.

lessons.title: Decorators with Arguments & functools.wraps
lessons.explain: A decorator factory is a function that takes arguments and returns the real decorator. Inside it, @functools.wraps(fn) copies the wrapped function's name, docstring, and metadata onto the wrapper so debugging and docs keep working.
takeaways: A decorator with arguments is really a factory: outer call takes args, inner function is the decorator.
Always apply @functools.wraps(fn) to your wrapper to preserve __name__ and __doc__.
The wrapper usually takes (*args, **kwargs) so it works with any signature.

quiz.q: What does @functools.wraps(fn) do inside a decorator?
options: Copies __name__, __doc__ and other metadata from fn onto the wrapper
Prevents the decorator from being applied twice
quiz.why: wraps updates the wrapper's metadata to look like the original function.

quiz.q: In the example, what does repeat(2) return?
options: A decorator: a function that takes fn and returns the wrapper
quiz.why: repeat(2) returns decorator, which is then applied to greet as @repeat(2).

quiz.q: Without functools.wraps, what would greet.__name__ be after decoration?
quiz.why: Without wraps, the name of the replacement function (wrapper) leaks through.

challenge.hint: tag('math') runs first and returns deco; deco then receives add.

lessons.title: Concurrency I: Threading Basics
lessons.explain: Threads let one program juggle several tasks that spend most of their time waiting, like downloads or file reads. You start them with threading.Thread, wait with join(), and protect shared data with a Lock.
takeaways: Threads shine for I/O-bound work, not CPU-bound number crunching (see the GIL lesson).
Always join() every thread you start so the main program waits for them.
Guard shared mutable state with threading.Lock to avoid race conditions.
lessons.code:
import threading

results = []
lock = threading.Lock()

def work(n):
    with lock:
        results.append(n * n)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work, args=(i,)) for i in range(5)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
print(sorted(results))

quiz.q: Why do we call t.join() on each thread?
options: To wait until the thread finishes before the program continues
To give the thread a higher priority
quiz.why: join() blocks the calling thread until that thread completes.

quiz.q: What is threading.Lock() used for?
options: Stopping two threads from mutating shared data at the same time
quiz.why: Only one thread can hold the lock, so the critical section runs atomically.

quiz.q: Threads in CPython are a poor fit for which workload?
options: CPU-heavy computation, because of the GIL
quiz.why: The GIL stops threads from running Python bytecode in parallel on multiple cores.

challenge.hint: join() guarantees every thread finished appending before the print runs.

lessons.title: Concurrency II: asyncio Basics
lessons.explain: asyncio runs many tasks on a single thread with an event loop. Coroutines declared with async def pause at await, letting other tasks run while they wait — no threads, no GIL fights.
takeaways: Write coroutines with async def and pause them with await.
asyncio.gather() runs coroutines concurrently and returns results in order.
asyncio.run(main()) starts the event loop from normal synchronous code.
lessons.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return "data:" + name

async def main():
    out = await asyncio.gather(fetch("a"), fetch("b"), fetch("c"))
    print(out)

asyncio.run(main())

quiz.q: What does await do inside a coroutine?
options: Pauses this coroutine so the event loop can run others until the awaited thing completes
quiz.why: await yields control back to the event loop instead of blocking.

quiz.q: asyncio.gather(a(), b(), c()) returns results in which order?
options: The order the coroutines were passed in
quiz.why: gather preserves argument order regardless of completion order.

quiz.q: Which call runs an async main() from regular code?
options: await main() at module top level
quiz.why: asyncio.run() creates the event loop, runs the coroutine, and closes the loop.

challenge.code:
import asyncio

async def double(x):
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    return x * 2

async def main():
    print(await asyncio.gather(double(1), double(2), double(3)))

asyncio.run(main())
challenge.hint: gather keeps the order of its arguments in the result list.

lessons.title: The GIL & Multiprocessing
lessons.explain: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, so threads can't speed up CPU-bound code. The multiprocessing module sidesteps the GIL with separate processes, each with its own interpreter and memory.
takeaways: The GIL means one thread runs Python bytecode at a time per process.
multiprocessing gives true parallelism for CPU-bound work via separate processes.
Processes don't share memory: data is pickled back and forth, so keep payloads small.

quiz.q: What does the GIL actually prevent?
options: Two threads executing Python bytecode truly in parallel
Two separate processes running at once
Using more than one CPU core for separate programs
quiz.why: The GIL is per-process; separate processes each have their own.

quiz.q: Why guard multiprocessing code with if __name__ == "__main__"?
options: So child processes re-importing the module don't spawn more children
It makes the code run faster
It is required for every Python script
quiz.why: On some platforms children re-import the module, which would re-execute the spawn code.

quiz.q: How do processes exchange data compared to threads?
options: They don't share memory; data is serialized (pickled) between them
They cannot exchange data at all
quiz.why: Each process has isolated memory, so arguments and results are pickled.

challenge.hint: Pool.map applies the function to each item and preserves input order.

lessons.title: Writing Your Own Context Managers
lessons.explain: Any class with __enter__ and __exit__ works with the with statement. __enter__ sets things up, and __exit__ always runs afterward — even when the block raises — making it perfect for cleanup.
takeaways: __enter__ sets up and usually returns the resource bound by 'as'.
__exit__ always runs: put cleanup there, not after the with block.
Return True from __exit__ to suppress an exception; return False (or None) to let it propagate.
lessons.code:
import time

class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        self.t0 = time.perf_counter()
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        self.elapsed = time.perf_counter() - self.t0
        return False

with Timer() as t:
    total = sum(range(1000))
print(t.elapsed >= 0)

quiz.q: When is __exit__ called?
options: Always: whether the block ends normally or raises
quiz.why: Guaranteed cleanup is the whole point of context managers.

quiz.q: How can a context manager suppress an exception from the with block?
quiz.why: A truthy return from __exit__ tells Python the exception was handled.

quiz.q: What does __enter__ typically return?
options: The resource that 'with ... as name' binds to
quiz.why: The as-target receives whatever __enter__ returns.

challenge.prompt: Fill in the blank so this prints: open
challenge.hint: The as-target receives whatever __enter__ returned.

lessons.title: Generators: send(), Coroutines & Pipelines
lessons.explain: Calling .send(value) on a generator feeds a value in as the result of the currently-paused yield expression. That turns generators into coroutines you can chain into lazy data-processing pipelines.
takeaways: yield both produces a value outward and receives the next send() value inward.
Prime a coroutine with next(gen) before the first send().
Chain small generators so each stage lazily transforms the stream.
lessons.code:
def averager():
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    while True:
        x = yield total / count if count else 0.0
        total += x
        count += 1

avg = averager()
next(avg)
avg.send(10)
avg.send(20)
print(avg.send(30))

quiz.q: In 'x = yield 10', what does gen.send(99) do?
options: Resumes the generator with x bound to 99
Restarts the generator from the top
quiz.why: send() resumes at the paused yield and the expression evaluates to the sent value.

quiz.q: Why call next(gen) before the first send()?
options: The generator must run to its first yield before it can receive a value
It is optional style with no effect
quiz.why: A just-created generator hasn't started; only None can be sent before the first yield.

quiz.q: What do generator-based pipelines buy you?
quiz.why: Each stage yields items on demand instead of building giant intermediate lists.

challenge.code:
def doubler():
    total = 0
    while True:
        x = yield total
        total += x * 2

g = doubler()
next(g)
print(g.send(5))
print(g.send(3))
challenge.hint: Trace it: after send(5), total is 0 + 5*2 = 10, which is then yielded.

lessons.title: Descriptors & the Descriptor Protocol
lessons.explain: A descriptor is any object defining __get__, __set__, or __delete__. Python calls these hooks automatically on attribute access — it's the machinery behind @property, @staticmethod, and most ORMs.
takeaways: Descriptors intercept attribute access via __get__ / __set__ / __delete__.
__set_name__ tells the descriptor which attribute name it was assigned to.
@property is just a convenient built-in descriptor.

quiz.q: Which methods make a class a descriptor?
quiz.why: Defining any of these hooks opts the class into the descriptor protocol.

quiz.q: In 'class Item: price = Positive()', when is Positive.__set__ called?
options: When the class body is defined
quiz.why: __set__ fires on attribute assignment; __get__ fires on reads.

quiz.q: What is @property built on?
quiz.why: property is a class implementing __get__/__set__/__delete__.

challenge.hint: Assignment triggers __set__; reading triggers __get__, which uppercases.

lessons.title: How Classes Work: type() & Metaclasses Intro
lessons.explain: Classes are objects, and type(name, bases, dict) is the call that creates them — class X: ... is syntax sugar for it. A metaclass is the class of a class: Python calls it to build every class, letting you customize class creation itself.
takeaways: type('X', (Base,), {...}) creates a class dynamically at runtime.
The metaclass of a normal class is type.
Metaclass hooks run at class-definition time, not when you instantiate.
lessons.code:
def init(self, v):
    self.v = v

Point = type("Point", (), {"__init__": init})
p = Point(5)
print(type(p).__name__, p.v)

quiz.q: What does type('A', (B,), {'x': 1}) return?
options: A new class named A inheriting B with class attribute x = 1
quiz.why: The three-argument form of type() is the class factory.

quiz.q: What is the metaclass of a normal class?
quiz.why: type is the default metaclass; classes are instances of type.

quiz.q: When does a metaclass's __new__ run?
options: When the class statement executes (class-creation time)
Each time you instantiate the class
Only when the metaclass module is imported
quiz.why: Metaclasses customize class creation, which happens once at definition.

challenge.code:
def init(self, v):
    self.v = v

K = type("K", (), {"__init__": init, "double": lambda self: self.v * 2})
print(K(21).double())
challenge.hint: The dict passed to type() becomes the class namespace: methods and all.

lessons.title: functools Toolkit: lru_cache, partial, reduce
lessons.explain: functools packs three high-leverage helpers: lru_cache memoizes expensive pure functions, partial freezes some arguments of a function, and reduce folds an iterable into a single value.
takeaways: @lru_cache(maxsize=None) memoizes pure functions: same args, instant answer.
partial(fn, a) returns a new callable with argument a pre-filled.
reduce(fn, iterable, start) folds left; pair it with the operator module for clean code.

quiz.q: What does @lru_cache do?
options: Caches return values so repeated calls with the same arguments are instant
Runs the function on multiple cores
quiz.why: It memoizes: a cache keyed by arguments stores past results.

quiz.q: What does partial(int, base=2) return?
options: A callable like int but with base pre-set to 2
quiz.why: partial freezes arguments, returning a new callable awaiting the rest.

quiz.q: reduce(operator.add, [1, 2, 3], 10) equals?
quiz.why: Start at 10, then 10+1+2+3 = 16.

challenge.code:
from functools import lru_cache

calls = []

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def f(x):
    calls.append(x)
    return x * 10

f(2)
f(2)
f(3)
print(len(calls), f(2))
challenge.hint: The second f(2) hits the cache, so the body runs only twice total.

lessons.title: Dataclasses: Less Boilerplate OOP
lessons.explain: The @dataclass decorator generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ from simple annotated field declarations. For mutable defaults like lists, use field(default_factory=list) — a plain [] default is rejected.
takeaways: @dataclass writes __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ for you.
Annotate each field; mutable defaults need field(default_factory=...).
Dataclass instances compare by value with ==, not by identity.

quiz.q: Why field(default_factory=list) instead of grades: list = []?
options: A plain [] would be shared across all instances
Lists are banned as defaults entirely
quiz.why: default_factory calls list() fresh for each instance; a literal default is one shared object.

quiz.q: Which methods does @dataclass generate by default?
quiz.why: Those three are the core boilerplate it writes for you.

quiz.q: Student('Ava', [80]) == Student('Ava', [80]) evaluates to?
quiz.why: The generated __eq__ compares field tuples, not identity.

challenge.prompt: Fill in the blank so this prints: Point(x=3, y=0)
challenge.hint: y needs a default value so it can be omitted.

lessons.title: Type Hints & Static Checking
lessons.explain: Type hints like def f(x: int) -> int document intent and let tools like mypy catch bugs before runtime. Python itself ignores them completely — they're metadata for humans and checkers, not enforcement.
takeaways: Hints are documentation plus tooling; Python never enforces them at runtime.
Use list[int], dict[str, int], and X | None for modern container and optional hints.
Run mypy or pyright in CI to catch type errors before they ship.
lessons.code:
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

print(add(2, 3))
print(add.__annotations__)

quiz.q: Does Python enforce type hints at runtime?
options: No: they are ignored at runtime; tools like mypy check them statically
quiz.why: Hints live in __annotations__; nothing checks them unless you run a checker.

quiz.q: What does add.__annotations__ hold?
options: The parameter and return annotations as a dict
Nothing: the attribute does not exist
quiz.why: Annotations are stored in a plain dict on the function object.

quiz.q: How do you hint 'a list of ints' on modern Python (3.9+)?
quiz.why: Builtin generics like list[int] work since Python 3.9.

challenge.hint: Hints are not enforced: 'x' + 'y' is perfectly valid string concatenation.

lessons.title: Logging Done Right
lessons.explain: The logging module replaces print-debugging with leveled, configurable output. Get a logger per module with getLogger(__name__), log at the right level, and configure handlers and formatting once at startup.
takeaways: Use logging.getLogger(__name__) per module instead of the root logger directly.
Levels ascend: DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL.
Configure once with basicConfig or dictConfig; library code should never print().
lessons.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("app")
log.debug("hidden")
log.info("started")
log.warning("careful")

quiz.q: With level=logging.INFO, which call produces no output?
quiz.why: DEBUG is below the INFO threshold, so it is filtered out.

quiz.q: Why prefer logging over print() for diagnostics?
options: Levels, timestamps, and routing to files or handlers without code changes
quiz.why: Logging separates the decision to record from where the record goes.

quiz.q: What does logging.getLogger('app') return on the second call?
options: The same logger object as the first call
quiz.why: Loggers are cached by name in a registry; same name, same object.

challenge.code:
import logging
log = logging.getLogger("demo")
print(log.name)
print(log.getEffectiveLevel() == logging.WARNING)
challenge.hint: A fresh logger inherits the default WARNING level from the root logger.

lessons.title: Debugging with pdb
lessons.explain: pdb is Python's built-in debugger: calling breakpoint() drops you into an interactive shell at that line. Step with n, continue with c, inspect values with p, and quit with q.
takeaways: breakpoint() starts a pdb session at that line (Python 3.7+).
n runs the next line, c continues, p <expr> prints a value, q quits.
Use pp for pretty-printing and l to see surrounding source.
lessons.code:
def divide(a, b):
    # breakpoint()  <- drop in here: try p a, then n, then c
    return a / b

print(divide(10, 2))

quiz.q: What does breakpoint() do?
options: Opens an interactive pdb session at that line
quiz.why: It invokes the built-in debugger right where it is called.

quiz.q: In pdb, what does the 'n' command do?
options: Executes the current line and moves to the next one
quiz.why: n means next: step over the current line.

quiz.q: How do you inspect a variable's value inside pdb?
quiz.why: p evaluates and prints the expression in the current frame.

challenge.prompt: If you put breakpoint() on the s += x line, pdb would show s as 1, then 3, then 6. What does the program print?
challenge.hint: The debugger only observes; the loop still sums 1 + 2 + 3.

lessons.title: Packaging: Ship Your Own pip Package
lessons.explain: Shipping a package means a pyproject.toml describing your project plus your code in a package directory. pip install -e . installs it editable for development, and python -m build plus twine take it to PyPI.
takeaways: pyproject.toml holds name, version, dependencies, and the build backend.
Keep importable code in a package directory with an __init__.py.
pip install -e . for local development; build with python -m build.
lessons.code:
# myapp/__init__.py
__version__ = "1.0.0"

def hello(name):
    return "Hello, " + name + "!"

print(__version__)
print(hello("pip"))

quiz.q: What does pyproject.toml describe?
options: Project metadata: name, version, dependencies, build system
quiz.why: It is the standard manifest pip and build tools read.

quiz.q: What does pip install -e . do?
options: Installs the local package in editable mode so changes take effect immediately
quiz.why: Editable installs link to your working directory instead of copying.

quiz.q: Where does importable package code live?
options: In a directory with an __init__.py (or a namespace-package directory)
quiz.why: The package directory is what Python puts on the import path.

challenge.code:
__version__ = "2.5.0"
major, minor, patch = __version__.split(".")
print(major, int(minor) + int(patch))
challenge.hint: split('.') gives ['2', '5', '0']; add the last two as integers.

lessons.title: Design Patterns in Python
lessons.explain: Design patterns are reusable solutions to common problems: Singleton (one shared instance), Observer (publish/subscribe), Factory (create objects without naming the class). Python often implements them with dunders, decorators, or first-class functions instead of heavy class hierarchies.
takeaways: Singleton: override __new__ to return the existing instance.
Observer: keep a list of subscriber callbacks and notify them on change.
Prefer simple Pythonic tools (functions, context managers) over heavyweight pattern machinery.

quiz.q: How does the Singleton ensure a single instance?
options: __new__ returns the existing instance instead of creating a new one
__init__ raises an error on second use
It relies on a global variable alone
Python does this automatically for all classes
quiz.why: __new__ controls instance creation, so it can return the cached object.

quiz.q: In the Observer pattern, what does the subject keep?
options: A list of subscriber callbacks to notify on changes
A deep copy of every object
quiz.why: Observers subscribe callbacks; the subject calls them when state changes.

quiz.q: What is the most Pythonic 'factory'?
options: A plain function that returns instances
quiz.why: Functions are first-class; a simple function beats pattern ceremony.

challenge.code:
class Config:
    _inst = None
    def __new__(cls):
        if cls._inst is None:
            cls._inst = super().__new__(cls)
            cls._inst.mode = "dev"
        return cls._inst

c1 = Config()
c2 = Config()
c1.mode = "prod"
print(c2.mode)
challenge.hint: c1 and c2 are the same object, so the mutation is visible through both.

lessons.title: SQLite Databases with Python
lessons.explain: The sqlite3 module is in the standard library and stores a full SQL database in one file — or in RAM with :memory:. Always use ? placeholders for values; never format them into SQL strings yourself.
takeaways: sqlite3.connect(':memory:') gives you a throwaway database for experiments.
Use ? placeholders to prevent SQL injection.
commit() persists writes; close connections with a context manager or try/finally.
lessons.code:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users (name TEXT, age INTEGER)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)", [("Ava", 30), ("Bo", 25)])
db.commit()
rows = db.execute("SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 26 ORDER BY name").fetchall()
print(rows)
db.close()

quiz.q: Why use ? placeholders instead of f-strings in SQL?
options: f-strings cannot be used with SQL
quiz.why: The driver safely escapes bound values; string formatting lets attackers inject SQL.

quiz.q: What does commit() do?
options: Persists pending writes to the database
quiz.why: Writes sit in a transaction until committed.

quiz.q: What is sqlite3.connect(':memory:')?
options: A temporary database kept in RAM
A connection to a remote server
quiz.why: :memory: is the special name for a private in-RAM database.

challenge.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE t (v INTEGER)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO t VALUES (?)", [(1,), (2,), (3,)])
n = db.execute("SELECT SUM(v) FROM t").fetchone()[0]
print(n)
challenge.hint: fetchone() returns one row tuple; [0] takes its first column.

lessons.title: Talking to APIs: requests & JSON
lessons.explain: The requests library turns HTTP into one-liners: requests.get(url).json() fetches a URL and parses the JSON body. Always set a timeout, check the status code, and parse defensively since APIs change shape.
takeaways: requests.get(url, timeout=10).json() is the core API-call pattern.
Always set a timeout and check response.status_code before trusting the body.
Parse defensively with .get() and defaults: API responses change.
lessons.code:
import json

# this is what requests.get(url).json() would hand you:
sample = '{"name": "Skillzify", "users": 1200, "tags": ["python", "learn"]}'
data = json.loads(sample)
print(data["name"], data["users"])
print(data["tags"][1].upper())

quiz.q: What does requests.get(url).json() do?
options: Fetches the URL and parses the response body as JSON
Sends JSON data to the server
Opens the URL in a browser
quiz.why: .json() decodes the response bytes into Python objects.

quiz.q: Why pass timeout=10 to requests.get?
options: So a hung server cannot freeze your program forever
It makes the server respond faster
It is required for JSON responses
quiz.why: Without a timeout, a dead server can block your call indefinitely.

quiz.q: How should you read a possibly-missing key from API JSON?
options: data['key'] and hope for the best
quiz.why: .get() avoids KeyError when the API shape drifts.

challenge.code:
import json
raw = '{"items": [{"id": 1}, {"id": 2}, {"id": 3}]}'
data = json.loads(raw)
print(len(data["items"]), data["items"][-1]["id"])
challenge.hint: Three dicts in the list; [-1] is the last one, whose id is 3.

lessons.title: Profiling & Optimization
lessons.explain: Profile before you optimize: cProfile shows where your program really spends time, and timeit gives trustworthy micro-benchmarks. Most real wins come from better algorithms, not micro-tweaks.
takeaways: cProfile plus pstats finds the actual hotspots: measure, don't guess.
timeit.repeat avoids one-off timing noise for fair comparisons.
Optimize algorithms first; readability beats cleverness everywhere else.
lessons.code:
import cProfile, pstats, io

def slow():
    return sum(i * i for i in range(10000))

pr = cProfile.Profile()
pr.enable()
slow()
pr.disable()
out = io.StringIO()
pstats.Stats(pr, stream=out).print_stats(1)
print("profiled ok")

quiz.q: What is cProfile for?
options: Measuring where your program spends its time
quiz.why: It records per-function call counts and cumulative time.

quiz.q: Why use timeit instead of time.time() around code once?
options: It repeats the measurement and reduces timing noise for stable results
It runs the code in parallel
quiz.why: Repetition plus setup control makes micro-benchmarks trustworthy.

quiz.q: What is the first rule of optimization?
options: Measure first: profile before changing anything
quiz.why: Guessing hotspots wastes effort; profilers show the truth.

challenge.code:
import timeit
t1 = timeit.timeit('"-".join(str(n) for n in range(100))', number=100)
t2 = timeit.timeit('"-".join(map(str, range(100)))', number=100)
print(t1 > 0 and t2 > 0)
challenge.hint: Both timings are positive durations, so the comparison is always True.

lessons.title: Capstone: argparse CLI Application
lessons.explain: argparse turns a script into a real command-line tool: positional arguments, --flags, help text, and type conversion come free. parse_args() reads sys.argv, but you can pass an explicit list when testing.
takeaways: add_argument defines positionals ('name') and optionals ('--shout').
type=int converts input; action='store_true' makes boolean flags.
--help is generated automatically from your help= strings.
lessons.code:
import argparse

def build_parser():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Greet someone")
    p.add_argument("name")
    p.add_argument("--shout", action="store_true")
    return p

args = build_parser().parse_args(["Ava", "--shout"])
msg = "Hello, " + args.name + "!"
print(msg.upper() if args.shout else msg)

quiz.q: What does add_argument('--shout', action='store_true') create?
options: A boolean flag that is False unless --shout is passed
quiz.why: store_true flips the default False to True when the flag appears.

quiz.q: How do you test argparse code without real command-line arguments?
options: You cannot: it only ever reads sys.argv
quiz.why: parse_args optionally takes the argument list, which makes it testable.

quiz.q: What does --help do for an argparse program?
options: Prints auto-generated usage from your declared arguments
quiz.why: argparse builds the help screen from your arguments and help= strings.

challenge.code:
import argparse
p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("x", type=int)
p.add_argument("--times", type=int, default=1)
a = p.parse_args(["5", "--times", "3"])
print(a.x * a.times)
challenge.hint: x becomes int 5, --times becomes int 3; multiply them.

lessons.title: Pythonic Idioms Masterclass
lessons.explain: Pythonic code leans on the language: comprehensions, zip, enumerate, any/all, unpacking, and context managers. These idioms are shorter, often faster, and instantly readable to experienced Python developers.
takeaways: Prefer comprehensions and any()/all() over manual accumulator loops.
Unpack with a, b = ... and a, *rest = ...; iterate pairs with zip and enumerate.
Idiomatic code is a feature: it signals intent to every Python reader.
lessons.code:
words = ["  Hello ", "WORLD", " python "]
clean = [w.strip().lower() for w in words]
print(clean)
pairs = dict(zip(["a", "b"], [1, 2]))
print(pairs)
print(any(x > 5 for x in [1, 9, 3]))

quiz.q: Which is the most Pythonic way to build a doubled list?
options: map() with a lambda stored in a variable
A while loop with a manual index
quiz.why: The comprehension states the transformation directly and idiomatically.

quiz.q: What does a, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4] bind?
quiz.why: The starred target collects all remaining items into a list.

quiz.q: Why is any(x > 5 for x in xs) better than a manual loop?
options: It short-circuits on the first match and reads as pure intent
quiz.why: any() stops early and the generator expresses the condition directly.

challenge.code:
data = [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 3)]
letters, nums = zip(*data)
print(letters)
print(sum(nums))
challenge.hint: zip(*data) unzips: first elements together, second elements together.
